BE KIND TO THYSELF. Comes the message from above— "As thyself, thy nelghbouitove." With myself so vexed I grow— Of my weakness weary so, Basler may I tolerate Iffy neighbour than myself not hate. Take not part of thee for whole. Thou art neighbour to thy soul; The ray from Beaten that gilds the clod • Love thou, for it comes from God. Dear thou with thy human clay Lest thou miss the heaven-sent ray.
E. S. MARTIN.

Pure self-denial is our good angel's hand, barring the gates of sin.—AW,ifullois. Self-denial enlightens and blesses thelsoul by freeing it from selflshness.—Hatilda Fletcher. No one can well believe that our piety is sincere when Our behaviour is loose and irregular in its little details. ;WAIT was admiring the fat boy at the show. a Maurine," he said, "what a kind mother he must have !" Self-denial is that which gives the martyr a crown of glow. and exalts the beggar above the dignity of a king. —l,,tstus. If we are in the habit of neglecting little things, we shall he constantly offending our families, our domestics, and the public. "Now, children, what is the name of the meal you eat in the morning ?" "Oatmeal," replies a precocious member of the class. . _ . . . .

Ida (of thirty-five summers) : "Doing up one's hair is for us girls at fifteen—a labour; at twenty-five—a plea- sure; at thirty-five—an art." Home Tooke, being asked by Genre* 111. whether he played at cards, replied, "No, your Majesty; the fact is, I cannot tell a king from a knave." "You are picturing a rather gloomy future for me, madam," he said to the fortune-teller. "Yes, sir," she replied, "but it's the best I can do for half-a-crown." Judge: "The jury will now withdraw and find a ver- dict?' Prisoner ! "They needn't withdraw on my AC- Count. They can stay here, so far as lam concerned." An indolent boy being asked by his teacher who came latest to school, replied—" Indeed, sir, I cannot; say, for I did not get here early enough to see." Which letter in the alphabet is of the utmost import- ance to a young lady, and why ?—The letter "i," be- cause upon it depends whether her life *ill be married er marred. "Stockings? Yee, ma'am. What number do you wear?" Customer: "What number? Why, two, of course. Do you take me for a centipede or a one- legged veteran?" Mrs. Brown: "And so your husband lost his lea; isn't it awful ?" Wife: "You may well say so. And it was ontylast week that he bought anew pair of boots— a pair, Mn. Brown." Every man who makes the honest endeavour to live his own life sooner or later strikes off the claims that bind him, and in making himself free becomes a liberat- ing force in the lives of others. It is true that we do not know what a day may bring forth; but the experience of life is sufficient to convince most of us that if we choose we can do much to modify and direct and control our life. Little four-year-old Cora did not want to learn to read, and her mother asked her what she would do if she were unable to read when she grew up. "I'll get my husband to read to me," was the reply. A Scot, being shown Niagara, was asked if he had ever seen aught so beautiful and strange. He replied— " Weel, for bonny, I'll no' say; but, eh, mon, for queer, I Imo* saw a pence& wi' a wooden leg at Peebles." Our lives are spent either in doing nothing at all, or in doing nothing to the purpose, or in doing nothing that we ought to do; we are always complaining that our days are few and acting as if there would be no end to them. An hotel located at Erie, Pennsylvania, is being adver- tised as follows :—" There is no gilt-edged business about this house, and if you want to eat pie with a knife you can do it without fear of being ostracised from society." Some leiee were discussing, in the presence of a well- known financier, the difference between the real and the ideal, and he was appealed to for his opinion. "The real," said the financier, "is a Spanish coin; the ideal is the Spanish bond." It is said that when General Grant was in Japan the Japanese Premier, Prince Bung, desiring to compliment the General by telling him that he was born to com- mand, tried it in English, with this result—" Sire, brave • General, you was made to order." The most complete pun in the records ol literature is produced on the following words, which were inscribed on a tea-chest :—" Ta doeet," which is the second person singular of the verb doeeo, to teach; and, when literally translated, becomes "Thou tea-chest." Wife (pleadingly) : "I'm afraid. George, you do not lore me as well as you used to do." Husband: " Why ?" Wife: "Because you always let me get up to light the fire." Husband: "Nonsense, my love! Your getting up to light the fire makes me love you all the more." There was once an Irish 'bus conductor to whom Cardinal Manning recommended the assumption of the pledge, strengthening the precept by an allusion to his own example. " Och, now, thin," replied the Hibernian, with characteristic archness, "maybe yer iminence naided it." His Eminence's rigtd asceticism renders the joke doubly spicy. Magistrate: "Prisoner, this is the seventh time you have appeared before me." Prisoner: "I know it, your Honour. Your Honour always was a favourite of mine, your are so just." Magistrate (mollified): "Well, I'll let you off this time, but don't come before me again." Pri- soner: "That's a heed sentence, your Honour, but I'll try to bear it without complaint." It is said of a gentleman that he had a passion for the purchase of second-hand furniture at auctions, and that in making "good bargains" he had filled his house with antiquated and alrnolt useless' articles. Upon one occa- sion, his wife took the responsibility, without consulting or apprising her husband, to have a portion of the least useful removed to an auction room. Great was her dismay and her extreme astonishment, when, on the evening of the day of sale, a majority of the articles came back to the house. The husband had stumbled into the auction room, and, not knowing his own furni- ture, had purehated it at a better bargain than at first. NAPOLEON'S Menony.—The Duke of Wellington used to laugh at the good memory ascribed to Napoleon, and thus explained his habit of' calling out soldiers by name: "One of his generals (Lobau) used to get ready for him a list of soldiers to be called out from each regiment, and FO Napoleon when opposite to it used to call out the name, and the man came forth—that was all. I also doubt the goodness of his memory, from the looseness and inaccuracy of his statements. In his works—l mean in all he has ever written—you never find a thine re- lated precisely as it happened. He seems to have "had no clear nor distinct recollection. Scarcely once has he ever tripped into truth !—Lord Stanhope. Irerneen MORALITY.—It is probable that nearly al who think of conduct at all think of it too much; it is certain we all think too much of sin. Wears not damned for doing wrong, but for not doing right; Christ would never hear of negative morality; thou shalt was ever His word, with which he superseded thou shalt net. To make our ides of morality centre on forbidden acts is to defile the imagination and to introduce into our judg- ments of our fellow-men a secret element of gusto. If a thing is wrong for us, we should not dwell upon the thought of it; or we shall soon dwell upon it with in- verted pleasure. It we cannot drive it from our minds —one thing of two: Either our creel is in the wrong and we must more indulgently remodel it; or else, if our morality be in the right, we are criminal lunatics and should place our persons In restraint. —Front Robert Lonis Stevenson's Christmas Sermon in Scribner's. ENGAGEMENT RlNGS.—Speaking of engagement rings, a French authority makes the following remarks :—" The first of the presents which must be given to an affianced) bride ought to be the engagement ring' this ring must fer ever he kept by her, it is the first openly allowed gage of love. It should be in perfect taste, and at the came time not inconvenient to V 0 owner. I would not choose the ruby, it is too showy, loud, and indiscreet; my taste inclines towards the sapphire and the diamond, of which the one dose not go well without the other. I should not choose a large sapphire surrounded by diamonds; I should ask our jeweller-artists to interlace in happy combination the sapphire and the diamond. The turquoise is also a tasteful stone, but when it is con- stantly worn it has the immense disadvantage of chang- ing its colour, and to this change most ladies attach a sad and sentimental superstition. It should, therefore, not be chosen for the first present which is to be worn and cherished while life lasts, and which is to remain from the days of youth when everything else is changed." A RELIABLE REMEDY.

THE RUNCORN PERJURY CASE. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday before Mr, J. Brundrit and Mr. G. L. Davies, a master Mariner named Henry Williams,was summoned to answer a charge of having, on the 27th March, wilfully and corruptly given false evidence on his examination on oath before His Honour Judge Ffoulkes.on the hearing of an action in which John 131undell, land- lord of the Three Crowns Beerlieuse, lin,g4st., was the plaintiff and Williams, the defendant.—Mr. Wynne Humphreys appeared for the complainant, and Mr. T. Shepherd Little, barrister-at-Law, Liver- pool (instructed by Mr. J. Burton) defended.—ln his opening statement Mr. Humphreys complained that Mr. Burton had neglected the ordinary court- esy of professional life in not haying given him any intimation that be had briefed counsel in the case, but " thrice armed is he who heti' his quarrel just," and it would take more than the legal acumen and persuasive eloquence of his friend Mr. Little combined to convince the Bench that the defendant was not guilty of the charge made against him. In August of last year, Thomas Smith, a fish dealer, borrowed the sum of £lO from Mr. H. Harrison, on a promissory note, and the defendant and John Blundell became sureties. Smith fell into arrear with his repayments, and Mr. Harrison took proceedings in the County. Court against Blundell, with the result that the latter had to pay £8 4s. ed. Blundell then took proceedings against the defendant to recover half of ihis amount. The defendant appeared to have consulted his solicitor, and a most remarkable defence was set up at the hearing of this case. Where that defence came from it was not for him to inquire,but it was a somewhat remarkable thing that a man in tho defendant's position should avail himself of such a highly technical legal defence as that laid down, that where a surety became bound at the request of a co-surety and not at the vequest of the borrower, the latter could not recover from the surety so bound. At tho County Court the defendant alleged that he became a surety only at the request of Blundell, and the judge gave a verdict in his favour. He would bring evidence to show that Thomas Smith asked Williams personally, and that he at once consented. In fact, he signed a note before Blundell, who denied ever having asked the defendant, or having had any conversation on the subject. When before the magistrates a week previous, Mr. Little made a statement that defendant was a man of sul-stanc.e, and that the complainant was a man of straw and not worth 6d.; yet it was strange that when the defendant was before the County Court his wife said he could not pay more than 2s. a month out of his scanty earnings. But poverty was no crime, and it was better to be poor and honest, than a man of substance he chance and a perjured liar.—Evidence was given by Thomas Jones, the usher of the Connty Court, and by his honour Judge Ffoulkes, who produced his notes of the defendant's evidence at the trial. Blundell and Thomas Smith also gave testimony flatly contradicting defend- ant's statement.—Mr. W. D. Jolliffe, registrar of the County Court, produced the minute book.—The defend- ant on being charged in the usual way, stated that his evidence before the jildge was quite true.—For the defence Mr. Little submitted that if the Bench could not rely upon the evidence of either Blundell or Smith, they ought not to send the defendant for trial. They ought to be satisfied that they were two witnesses of good repute whom a jury might believe,anil ,in that case they had not two witnesses of good repute. He pointed out several contradictions on material points in the evidence of Blundell and Smith, and commented strongly upon the fact that they did not appear at the hearing of the County Court action. His friend Mr. Humphreys in his opening statement gave a remarkable suggestion which reflected little credit upon his know- leJge of the law of surety for it was a well-known fact that if a surety signed at the request of another surety, he was not liable, and if such a defence took his friend by surprise he ought to have applied for a new trial.— Bose Taylor was called and said she had heard Smith say that he would swear his life against Williams, but the Bench rejected this evidence.—The magistrates did not consider there was sufficient prima facie evidence to support a conviction and the case was dismissed.

div.head: CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &c.
div.p: CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &c.

" Peter Parley's annual for Boys and Girls, is to hand (from the firm of Mr. 13en George, 47, Hatton Garden, London), and, as usual, it is as handsome as it is interesting. There are too many gift books at the present day that are all outside show ; they are very nice as to binding and illustration, but when you have said Oat you have said all that is to be said. But Peter Parley's Annual is not of this class. It is certainly as to appearance one of the most attractive books published; binding and frontis- piece are alike works of art; but they are no more than a fine entrance to a beautifully furnished house. The An.sual has now reached its forty- eighth year of publication; but it is woung and fresh as ever. The stories &c. are as follows: Pile of strength ; Sleep and Dreams; The Black Bloodhound; Run Away; Christopher Columbus; The Quartermaster's Story,-and At School with the Blue Noses. As Peter Parley is "an old hand "he knows not only. what sort of tales boys and girls like, but what are, at the same time, good for them, and we can promise those who read these stories that they will not tire of them. They are illustrated of course, the _pictures this year being finely printed in monotint. "A Christmas Posy " is the title of a children's book published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. It is from the pen of Mrs. Molesworth who is experi- enced in work of this kind, and quite understands the tricks and manners of little folks. The titles of the stories are :—Grandmother Dear's old watch; My Pink Pot,; An honest Little Man; The six poor little princesses; Basil's Violin; the Missing Bon- bons : Lost Rollo ; and the Blue Dwarfs. There are numerous illustrations, ,and, as the pictures are, from the pencil of Mr. Walter Crane, it is a matter of course to say that they are of a high class. We have also to hand from Messrs. Macmillan and Co., the following volumes of their English Men of Letters, edited by Mr. John Morley:— London, by Sidney. Colvin ; De Quincey, by David Masson; Locke, by Thomas Fowler; and Words- worth, .by E. W. H. Myers. These volumes are issued at the low price of one shilling each. They are invaluable as critical biographies, for each author is dealt with by a writer specially qualified; and facts and discoveries of all kinds are brought down to the latest date. It is needless to say that works of this kind are admirable as gift books to , the studious.

"Christmas Arrows" is the title of the Quiver Annual. It is a sixpenny issue, well-illustrated, and contains a number of complete stories, with a Christmas Carol, by Dr. Mackenzie. Casaell's Illustrated Almanac for 1889, is another bright publication which is always welcome; the pictures alone are well worth the sixpence which is charged for tke almanac. The Magazine of Art for Decemer has for frontis- piece a photogravure ef Woodville's picture— " Saving the Guns at Maiwand." This reproduction Is a really powerfal and charming piece of work. Amongst the illustrated articles we have "Art in the Theatre," Alfred Gilbert, A.R.A.; Salisbury Hall, the Liverpool Collection, Expression in Drapery, Portraits .of D. G. Rosetti, Statue to General Gordon, &c.

The current issue of The Woman's World is a more than usually strong number. There is a notable paper, with portraits, of Madame De Maintenon ; In the Franciacorta, is also strikingly illustrated. The frontispiece is a pretty picture of a fancy dress ball; and there is "A note in some Modern Poets," by the editor—Mr. Oscar Wilde. -

The 'World of Adventure (part 3) promises to prove a wonderfully entertaining volume. It shows that fact is often stranger than fiction. The illus- trations are as striking as the text. Cassell's Family Magazine, the Quiver, and Little Folk, for December, are in no ways lacking; they reach us month by month "ever charming—ever new." We have also received from the same firm Part 11 of the Dore Milton; Part 35 of Illustrated Shakespeare; the Encyclopcedic Dictionary, Part 59; Familiar Wild Flowers, Part 34; Dictionary of English History, Part 14; and Part 17 of "The Sea: its stirring story of adventure, peril, and heroism."

div.head: AN ECCENTRIC WARRINGTON FLATMAN,
div.p: AN ECCENTRIC WARRINGTON FLATMAN,

A Wolverhampton oontemporary gives currency to the following item, which was published in August, 1839, and will be of interest to our readers: —"An 'oddity' of the name of Leigh, who for some years filled the honourable position of master of a flat navigating the river Mersey, and by Industry and a rather more than ordinary share of good luck' has accumulated a small independence, is spending his latter days in Warrington, in mak- ing preparations for his funeral, which, to appear- ance, seems to occupy the whole of his thoughts. Some years ago he procured a large oak chest, fastened with secret springs, in which his mortal remains were, after death, to be deposited, but that idea has been abandoned, and a new coffin has been procured. In shape it is a beautiful model of a pleasure yacht, and was built by Mr. Clare, of Sankey, of old English plank, lin. thick. It is provided with main- foresail, jib, and gaff-topsail, and on the stern is inscribed the name Admiral Nelson.' In length it measures 8 feet 2 Inches. Last week it was brought into Warrington, mounfed on wheels, and accompanied by its owner and a fiddler, and followed by a crowd of wondering spectators. Its final destination is at present fixed upon to be St. James's Cemetery at Liverpool, to which place' on its bill of lading' being complete, it is to be drawn by horses, and followed bv a certain number of John Leigh's fellow-flatmen, for whose refreshment on the way a large cask of ale is to be placed on the deck of the vessel. John Leigh's tombstone is also provided. It is ornamented by a picture of the flat Victory, and a rude representation of tile sun, moon, and stars. Underneath are some twenty lines of poetry, of which the last four may be taken as a specimen. They run as follow May God be our pilot, and steer us the right way; And all our fleet anchor in Heaven's bright bay ; The seas I have seen, and the ships I have passed: But the Lord will call us all down to our graves at last," From what can be ascertained it is doubtful whether the wishes of this eccentric person were carried out BO far as his desire to be buried at Liverpool is concerned, for it is stated that his remains were interred at ; Warrington.

CHARTErt XXVI.
"I WISWt COULD '

The world was nearly a year older, and Ursula was again in London. Dr.-Havarti had recom- mended the change when he saw how determined she was' to keep up bravely in her anxiety about Ray- mond,and how her health was breaking down with disquieting dreams after leap; blanks of sleeplessness. I won t pity you," he said, "for I know you will 'hate my pity, and it would only make you worse, but I must send you away if I want you to get well."

Margaret Havard and Mrs. Wilson were both so sorry for her that they refrained from giving her their usual doses of advice. Neither of them could be expected to admit with Hubert Allston that they liked the old merry-hearted, contradictory Ursula, with all her irritating, freaks, and her faculties on the alert, better than this new phase of a listless, almost meek young woman, liable to fits of terrible insomnia. It was not exactly that the old ladies mutually agreed to let her "gang her own gait," but they began to feel it was somewhat dangerous to attempt to remodel nature. The consequence was that the elasticity of the girl's disposition quickly re-asserted itself under different influences, and she soon became a marked figure in a sort of. Bohemian society—which gathered round her, as she said, in her old joking way, by a kind of "elective allinity"—and was act- mired and believed in by many, and criticised by others who wondered what this picturesque-looking heiress had to do amongst theiree and easy people who talked to her about their books and their paint- ings, or played sonatas and sang comic songs in her apartments. From the time she began to "receive," as they called it, with nobody but Mrs. Wilson to act propriety, careful chaperons shook. their heads because there wa.s no such thing as any very formal presentations in her reception-rooms. For a very young woman to refuse to be presented at Court, to declare she would not be attired by the •Iceepted milliner, who dressed "everybody else," and to repel some of the "best" people by coldness of manner, while she put on the airs of a beneficent angel to others who had no further qualification than that they were skilful pianists or artists, Was enough to create a prejudice against her. The stories went about of how she had wrung the hand of a working man—who had an unhealthy, pallid face, and a stooping figure, and whose expenses in Parliament were actually paid for by a Liberal club—with a sort of encouraging giip, while she held 'out a couple of fingers only to the Hon. Mrs. Shelling- ton, who hail invited a poor German lady to one of her parties for "lions," and had allowed the "lioness" to trudgehome shiveringthrough the snow in thin even- ing dress, bemuse the latter could not afford to pay the expense of a cab. The foreigner,who had nothing more to recommend her • than rapid, skilful, and clear execution up and down the keys of the piano, hadnearly died of inflammation of the lungs, and Miss Campion had complicated matters by. taking her in and nursing her, with Mrs. Wilson's assistance, till she was better.

The affair got somehow into the papers and made a disagreeable stir, with the addition of attracting attention to the young heiress which was probably, as other ladies said, exactly what she wanted. And Mrs. Wilson, who watched the admiration tinctured with sarcastic comment which the girl excited— half with pleasure and half with fear, which almost amounted to foreboding—wrote to tell the Havards "how Ursula was again getting talked about." To have her name in the papers was in the eyes of those ladies of a former generation something very like a hideous offence, though Ursula attached no im- portance to it whatever. But when the good doctor hurried to town as soon as he could spare half-a-day , from his practice, and saw that Ursula knew how to assume a mask of calm highbred gracefulness,that she was too wise to have her head turned by the attentien she excited; too utterly unself-conscious to care for meaningless strictures, he msured the terrified ladies that they might set their hearts at rest. He chuckled a little to himself when he saw that he had not preached against pinched waists and high-heeled shoes in vain, and that she had a style of her own which, in its strange mixture of fashion and simplicity discarding crinoettes, flounces' and furbelows—reminded him of the drapery of Greek sculpture. "You may trust her to hold her own even in London society,' he said, with a satisfied nod. "She is not a woman to be put in a wrong - position by anyone if she does not choose." ' The fine contempt which curved her lips shewed to advantage the delicate outlines of her quivering nostrils when she said, "I hate commonplace flatterers," and was sufficient tokeep her from 'being injured by open compliments which were net always in the bast taste. Other women might #nd a mistake of that sort easy to forgive. In Um grand campaign, by their eon- quests and flushed with anccess, they might receive billet-doux from one man and make rendezvous with another "just to amuse themselves," as they said In this easy Bohemian sol 4 but not so Ursula. It was one of the jokes about her that 3}lo was accustomed to say to men, "Mind, no compliments must enter Into friendship," and when this way of hers began to be understood, men were very ready with their offers of friendship. Fielding was in London just at this time, "poking about," as the doctor said, amongst "working men of all shades of opinion,and trying to turn the seamy side of life inside out." It was fortunate that the doctor credited him with coolness and sagseity„ though he did not altogether approve. "No bob- bies," as Da-Havari .famed "were so dangerous as charitable hobbies, no crochets such mistaken ones as those which were mixed up with so-called philan- thropy." But whatever his crotchets might be, Fielding was too courageously bent on the " bobbies " by Which ..he hoped to accomplish his little stroke of work in his generation to have much time to spare for the doctor's criticisms, or even to visit Ursula. The miscellany of people who surrounded her jarred upon his mood; he was weary of the tiresome list of her admirers—unable to believe that she valiantly strove to close her cars to such flatterers. Yet more than once he said to himself, " can't think what that look means she has got in her eyes—she never used to have it,"c and felt drawn by the old spell to scorch his wings by the tempting flaw. It was impossible for him to know how little she oared, when he heard that the breath of scandal was already beginning to touch her: He then went to her with enthusiasm, longing to tell her that lie was with her, though she might be alone Against the world—that, in fact, he was always' with her, and would never believe anything against her, not -though the seven angels shouted it through the seven trumpets into his ears. Ho found his par- tizanship was quite unneeded. She was altogether unaware that there was any calumny to be lived down, and he was conscious of a revulsion of feeling when he saw the sort of magnificence in which she was living. It was a sultry evening. Not a breath of air bad been stirring all day in one of the hot courts/ in the neighbourhood of Whitechapel in which he had been working, but by the time he had left it the wind had risen, and the dust which bad lain unswept for day after day was settling down on the oppressed lungs of the poor inhabitants. He had become so accustomed to the crazy staircases and the groaning board p of the back slums,,that Ursula's rooms seemed to him far More luxurious than they actually were. " She was sensible of the unusual reserve, if not actual coldness, which seemed to have fallen like a veil between them. She tried her old jokes and laughed her merriest. I suppose I must be leaving in about another month," she said, "as they tell me there will they be I no one in town." - 1 -

The speech did not seem natural to her, and he answered a little safcastically, "The way London i neople have of talking, as if there is no one n town, when there are only between three or four millions of toiling human creatures in it 1" 'And you are intending to remain amongst the toiling creatures ?" She suddenly remembered that someone had told her Mr. Fielding was getting a name for being a great philanthropist, and that that sort of thing was almost always great humbng. "I am hoping to find my work here for the present. To tell you the truth, work is not easy to find." " I thought you had the choice of all the profes sions, and that on would be splendidly equipped for any of them." He smiled again—rather a smile of self-deprecation than one of irony. _ _ _
"The Oxford life," he said, " leaves a man too old for three-fourths of the professions." "There is the Bar." '
"The refuge for the destitnte. I am at the Bar, but only in name. If you knew how many men come

THH PARMILL Imaimir.—At Tuesday's sitting of tlie Parnell Commission the evidence was confined almost exclusively to County Mayo. District Inspector Fitz- simoti gave formal evidence of finding notices at Cross- molina calling on the people to avoid a former witness named Hogan;' and District Inspector IVPArdle, stationed at Swinford, produced notices warning people not to pay rent on pain of social ostracism, the notices being signed by Patrick Egan. Witnesses were next called regardhig a series of outrages. David Freely detailed the circum- stances under which his son was murdered, but declined to say that the Land League had anything to do with the murder. Among the other witnesses was John Dillon, of Ballyhaunis, who said his father was shot dead after attending some evictions in 1881, and that he found a letter on his father, threatening him with death because of his action as agent. He did not hear the doctor say at the inquest that ' the wound was caused by a military or constabulary bullet. On Wednesday the cross-examination of Miss Lucy Thompson, landowner and agent, Castleisland, was con- tinued. She said she thought the Land Court was unfair in many instances. The tenants were able to take care of themselves, and in several cases were paying too little rent. Mr. Edward Moore Richards, of Enmscorthy, a landlord, said he was on good terms with his tenants before the establishment ef the local branch of the Land League, when tenants who paid their rents had to do so secretly. Captain Boycott, late agent on Lord Erne's estate, was net examined, and narrated the circum- stances which eventually compelled him and his family to leave Ireland altogether. This witness was not cross- examined, and several witresses substantiated the cap- tain's evidence. District-Inspector Gamble afterwards gave evidence as to boycotting and outrages at Tralee, and the Court adjourned On Thursday, Mr. S. Smith, an of the agent for the-Marquis of Sligo said he and his father were shot at near Clogherin 1879 by men with blackened faces. Witness returned the fire and shot one man dead. A herdsman in the employ of Mr. Smith said he was visited at night for buying turf of a boycott- ed farmer, and theshock to his wife was se great that she went mad and died in an asylum. Ames Buckley stated that he lived at Causeway, near Tralee, and in November, 1880, was sworn in as a member of a secret society called"the Fenian Brethren. He was cross- examined with a view to proving that his testimony was untrustworthy.

FOREIGN NEWS.

GENERAL BOULANGER. General Boulanger, in announcing his decision to sit for the department of the Nord, describes the Chamber of Deputies as an assembly of incapables. The Boulangists held a conference at St. Die, on Mon- day, but the delegates were received with a counter- demonstration, which resulted in a conflict, necessitat- ing the interference of the police. Several persons were injured. Pants, SATURDAY.—M. de Freycinet. Minister of Wan, has placed Capt. Driant, General Boulanger's son-in-law, under arrest for a month, for publishing a book without the previous sanction of his military superiors. CURIOUS RESURRECTION CASE.

Another curious "resurrection case" has eulivene,l he inhabitants of Vaise, near Lyons. A few days ago a well-to-do inhabitant of the town fell into a trance, and was officially certified to bo dead as a door-nail. Pre- parations were made tor the funeral, when, ors the night before the mournful event will to take place, tho sup- posed dead man sat up in his coffin and called for a drink. The person who was watching by the side of the reputed corpse was alarmed, and ran away, so the rather substantial ghost got out of his coffin, imbibed the con- tents of a bottle of wine which was on a table, divested himself of his grave-clothes, donned his own, and then woke up the members of his family. Next day, amid great revelry and rejoicing, the local Lazarus wont to the Mayor's office and reported hiniseif "alive and kicking." END OF A BRIGAND CHIEF.

A short time ligo the Hungarian gendarmerie sur- rounded the Danube island of Ostrovo, where a re- nowned brigand chief had taken refuge. The latter, who had previously escaped half a dozen times from prison, managed to get away from Ostrova and rendk Posarevatz, in Servia. There he sought refuge with his wife's parents, but they refwed to afford him hospi- tality. Thereupon he threatened them n with a pistol, hut before be had time to fire his father-in-law shot Lint dead with a revolver, and then went immediately to re- port whet had happened to the gendarmerie. The brigand chief had been condemned to death, and a reward of 200 ducats had been set on his head. DISASTROUS EXPLOSION AND FIRE.— TEN LIVES LOST.

NEW YORK, TUESDAY MORNING—About two o'clock this morning, an explosion occurred at Oliver's Oatme4l Mill, Chicago, and was immediately followed by fire. Ten persons lost their lives either by the explosion or in the flames. Seven of these were operatives oa the pre- mises, the others being occupants of HA adjoiming tene- ment dwelling. The cause of the explosion is not known, but it is supposed to be due to the bursting of a boiler. DESPERATE RIOT IN ALABAMA.

NEW Yon, SPNDAY.—At Birmingham, in Alabama, to-day, a furious mob attacked the gaol with the object. of lynching a man named ITawes who was imprisoned on suspicion of having muriler;id his wife and twa r7aughters for the alleged purpose of marrying again. The body of the woman was found at Ow I;attora of a lake, with her head cut open, as if with an axe, and iron weights, amounting to 2001b3., had been tied to her head and feet. The evidence against the tnsbancl was strong, and all the statements he made we,re prove,: to be untrue. Consequently a keen feeling was aroused against him throughout the community, an many threats were made to lynch him. The gaol in which ho was cenifined was therefore doubly guarded. About 12 o'clock on Saturday night a mob went to the gaol howl ing and demanding the release of Howes. The officers refused to give up their prisoner, and commanded the mob to halt. This order they faile I to obey; and the officers fired on them with rifles and pistols. The shots were returned, and the firing 00n0tinues1 from both sides for 15 minutes to half an hour. None of the officers were injured, but over 20 of the mob were either killed or wounded. The Sheriff's guard is now in possession of all the streets leading to the gaol. The Sheriff gave the orders to fire, and it is said he turned a (lading gun on the mob. The Postmaster of the town, a man named Throckmorton, is reported to be among the killed._

Tim 'YORK, MONIDAY.—BesitIeA the -Sheriff, the Police Chief has also been detained in custody for nis action in firing on the mob yesterday at ltirmiaeham. i"C-A-A-13f7iTITRDAY.—allonels Kitchener and Barrow. with the Egyptian cavalry, to-day reconmitrod the enemy's position, getting well behind the rear of the Arab trenches. The were charged by the rebel horse- men and compelled to fall back, covered by the fire of the forts, losing one man killed and two wounded, The Damanhoor has arrived with the remainder of the Scot- tish Borderers on board.

SCAKIII, SUNDAY.—The StiPbePrl arrived from Kassa, with the Soudaness battalion on board. General Gren- fell today personally reconnoitred the enemy's position. The troops are in good health. A fresh demand for reinforceseents'has'been made by telegram to-day to the ' authorities in London. Sumac, Motmar EVEVING.—The offensive operation, began this morning, a heavy artillery fire being opened by all the forts on the-enemy's redoubts. The practice was excellent, endthe whole of the enemy's works soon showed evidence of the effects ,of the concentrated fire kept up upon them,-tho redoubt on the right, which was specially extoaed to the fire of the 64-pounder mounted by the sailors on Saturday, being very greatly damaged A large number of officers and men and manr of the Inhabitants ef the town assembled to watch the effects of the fire, and the Arab population appeared greatly impressed with the weight and power of the big gun A few pieces of this calibre would tend very greatly to secure Suakim in the future from renewed attacks by the enemy. This afternoon the rebels, as if to show that they were in no way dispirited by the results of the bombardment of their works, 'fired several shells from the redoubt on their left. One of them fell in Fort Gamaza and slightly wounded a soldier. Preparations are being made for the treatment of the wounded in the coming engagement, and for this purpose the Shibeen has been taken up as a hospital ship. It is calculated that she will afford accommodation for 118 British officers and men.,

EXECUTION OF A t4EYT (JAG ENARIAN. •At Worcester. on et,day, Sathnel Crowther, shoe- maker, 71, was executed for the murder of John Will's at Droitwich, on August let. The convict, being a cripple, and bent almost double by age and work, was atlowou to hobble with a stick across the prison yard to the place Of execution. When he had been pinioned by Berry. the old man was supported on the scaffold by the executioner's assistant. The drop was 3ft. 6in. Death was instantaneous. The culprit was visited on Friday and• Saturday by relatives, but he exhibited no contrition. —Crowther was aroused at six o'clock, and a few minutes later the Rev. A. Telfer was in attendance, and remained with him to the last. Be listened with an- parent attention, and fully confessed his crime. He took breakfast at seven o'clock, and at 'eight asked for some beer. This, however, not being handy, some brandy was given him. A few minutes before eight the usual prooession was formed to the scaffold, where Berry was the executioner. On Berry pulling the cap over his face he requested that it might be removed, but in another moment the drop was withdrawn, and he apparently died without a struggle.

THE WHITECHAPEL MURDERS. The police are continuing inquiries into the antecedents of Joseph Isance, said to be a Polish Jew, who is now in custody on a charge of watch stealing. Mary Cusins, the deputy of a lodging-house in Paternoster-row, near Dorset‘street, and Cornelius Oakes, a lodger, state that the conduct of the prisoner was frequently strange. Although he had a violin and four or five other musical instruments, he was never known to play any of them. Oakes says the prisoner used often to change his dress. He heard him threaten violence to all women above 17 years of age. • The Star understands that an appalling discovery has been made in connection with the Whitechapel murders which explains the method and the motive of the criminal, while it leaves his identity as mysterious as ever.

The hon member told the oft-repeated tale of the bad housing and inadequate pay of the national school teachers In the sister isle. ?le related how Administration after Ad- nistratien had promised redress for admitted grievances awl had failed to perform those promiaes until it had become a weary task to recapitulate these complaints— weary alike to the members who brought the matter forward and to these who had to listen. Mr. COttWAY nailed attention to the unsatisfactory sanitary condition of the schools, and urged that better buildinr,s should be provided for educational purposes. Twioe as much money, he said, was spent on the police in Ireland as was expended on education there. £1,300,000 was spent on the police and £750.000 on edu- cation. That fact had only to be mentioned to condemn the system which prevailed in Ireland. The pay of the teachers, he considered, demanded the attention of the Government .

div.head: EAST AFRICA AND SUAKIN.
div.p: EAST AFRICA AND SUAKIN.

Mr. J. MORLEY asked whether the Government had any information as to a statement to the effect that certain place on the Fast Coast of Africa had been utterly ruined and destroyed, which two months ago was the most nrosperous town on the East Cost? MT. W. H. SMITH replied that informatics" had reached the Government as to the occurrence to which the right hon. gentleman referred, but the report was of the most meagre character, and he thought it would he on the whole more satisfactory to postpone the question. Mr. Joint MORLEY asked if it was true, as stated in the newspapers', that demands for fresh reinforcements had reached the Government from Suakim ?

Mr. SraNnoeg said the Government had reoeived the following telegram from General Dormer dated Cairo, December 9th "Grenfell fully understands, and tele- graphs his opinion of confidence, hut, in the face of re- peated offers of reinforcements, thinks he might not be justified in continuing refusal Therefore, an Egyptian steamer will be ready to leave Suez about December 12. I propose to send her back to Suakim with a equadran of the 12th Hussars and 300 men of the Welsh Regiment." These steps had been approved. in another telegram General Greaten says I am quite confident of success." It miglit interest the House to know that there were new at Suakim 110 Mounted British Infantry, and over 800 British Infantry, and the total force, including Egyptian troops, was over 6.500. The last report RS to the forees opposed to us, stated the number at, 1,700, of which 700 were stated to be in reserve at Flatitioub.

Replying to a further question by Mr. J. Morley. Mr. STANHOPE said that her Majesty's Government them. selves originally offered reinforcements to the force which-General Grenfell was about to take to Suakim. SUPPLY.

div.head: ANOTHER WOMAN STABBED. ._
div.p: ANOTHER WOMAN STABBED. ._

About half-past two on Tuesday morning, a man named MOMS Wood was accosted in Daistomlane by a woman, who told him she had been stabbed. He ob- tained assistance, and the woman, whose name is Clara Moore, was taken to the German Hospital close by, from which she was discharged after her wound had been dressed. Her assailant could not be found. It was at first suspected that the East End murderer had been at work again, but inquiries tended to show that the affair is the out Come of a street brawl.

INTEMPERANCE GUARD. —A wealthy American Lady whose only son was fcs years a slave to intemperance, after seeking in vain for a cure, mid trying all known remedies, at last found a simple means that cured and save him from a drun- kard's gvare. Anyone snffering or desiring to help others in this worthy cease, by tending a self-addressed stamped en- velope to Mr. James Holland, 25, Hark-st., High Holborn, London, will receive this information free of charge. Men- tion this paper.—Ada.. WIFE IiCEDER.—Af the Leeds Assizes, on Thursday, Charles Bulmer, a groom, who was found guilty of murdering his wife at Huddersfield, was sentenced to death. The man inflicted four deadly wounds on his wife's throat with a razor, and then presented it to a friend. Surcins n; A Rent Tun.—About seven o'clock on Thursday morning the body of Mary Curtis, aged 43, was found in a rain tub at the rear of her house in Leek. She was in a sitting position, and only a night dress on. The deceased was the wifeof a coachman, who is unable to assign reason for the rash act. Tim HAVANT MURDER.—The inquest was resumed on Wednesday on the body of the boy Seal, who was murdered recently at Havant. Professor Tidy said it would be extremely difficult to suppose that the fatal wound could be inflicted without the hand or clothes of the murderer being stained. Considerable force must have been used. Robert Husband, prisoner's father said he sent his son at five minutes past six to get some money from Mrs. Farnden. He returned at 6.20 saying that a murder had been committed. Witness saw no blood on his hands. The Coroner, in summing up, said the superintendent of police had tried to prove motive, but it was for ' the jury to decide on that point. After two hours and a half's consideration the jury founl a verdict of" Wilful murder against some person unknown,"

A soldier at Faure put on a shirt hi which lurked a needle. The needle entered the heart, and he died. Just sae drop of blood trickled from the wound.

A hundred men have been thrown out of employment by the flooding of the Boater Nouse Colliery, Glasgow. Three persons are known to be drowned in the lower seam. .

He survived the aocident only an hour. Robertson had just rot an engagement on a news- paper in the south of England. Sampson Low and Co. for the alleged premature publication of Sir Morell liackertzie's book, has been delivered. The publishers claim an injunction and damages, the amount of which is not stated.

Our home pig-breeders must be on the lookout, for the Danes are busily engaged experimenting as to the best variety of pig for bacon, and they have been pros- pecting among the carers on this side also. It will not be the American trade that will suffer from this com- petition, but our home-growers, for bh• Danish plan is to market only the best. At Derbyshire A MIMS, on Moray, Joe. !Tiger's, joiner, was indicted for the wilful murder erfJamPs Barlow. of Swaisby, near Ashby-de-la-Zouch, en Anyt 4th, by stabbing him during general quarrel outside a public- house on the lost day of a village wake. The jury found a verdict of " Mans/aughter." and Mr. Justice Cave sen- tenced the prisoner to 10 years' penal servitude.

THE ROIIIIRICY OF • MAIL BAS.—Plerbert James Lead- beatter, aged 21 years, railway porter, was sentenced at Leeds Assizes, on Monday, to 18 months' hard labour for stealing the mail bag at Morley station on September 12, containing jewelry, Marrs, securities, and other articles, of the aggregate value of £6.000, the property of the Poettnaster-General. The prisoner pleaded guilty.

_ Three men were badly injured at the new London and North-Western Railway Works, Hindlow, Buxton, on Tueseay, by an explosion of gelatine cartridge. dor ng blastiing operations. A man named Smith had most of tip- flesh blown off his face and lost one leg, and Jas. Hurst and Matthew Renshaw received injuries to the head and body. The explosion is said to have been caused by using an iron rammer to charge the hole. On Saturday morning, a shocking fatality occurred at Flockton Pit, at' Barrow Collieries, Worsborough, near Barnsley. A miner, named Thomas Roes, was crushed to death by a large fall from the roof. Deceased, who resides in Henry-street, Worsborough Bridge, leaves n widow and eight small children. His companion left him for a short time, and on returning to the working pleoe found him buried alive under some stone, death ensuing before he was extricated. DamnTs.—The wife of John Dransfield, a police officer belonging to the Bradford force, gave birth nn Saturday to three male children at one birth. One of them lnis since died, but the other children, fine boys, ore, with the mother, doing well.—The wife of a labour- ing man living.at Sandbnrst, Berke, named Mason. has given birth to triplets, all tine healthy girls. The father has been out of work for some months, and there are five other children. The mother and daughters are doing welL .

. - THE WIMPY( Trrrrn Aarrarroar.—Ten days' notices were on Monday served by the representatives of Christ Church, Oxford, upon the tithepayers in the Meifod Valley, Montgomeryshire, for nrnars of tithe rent. A large number of the farmers have not paid the tithe since 1386, when strong oontingents of police, to the number of 300, were drafted into the valley to enforce the sales. The Dean and Ctiarter of Christ Church re- fuse to concede an abatement of 10 per cent., and so the tithepayers have determined to resist.

_ Many of the American railroads employ female labour extensively, and it is found That for certain kinds ol work young women are better adapted than young men. The wages they receive are from 20dol. (£4) to 55d01. (£11) per month, which is from one-half to three-fourths of the pay of men for the same class of work. The superior rapacity of the American girl for railway work, as compared with her English sister, is no doubt accounted for by the fact of her education better fittinf her for busioess life.—ltailtra.v Press.

Frank Grafton, aged 14 years, living with a family named Brown, et Plumstead, on Saturday was handling a revolver, which he supposed to be unloaded, belonging to a lodger, when he pulled the trigger, and a bullet entered the head of a httle boy named Brown, causing injuries which resulted in death in three hours. Mrs. Brown, he mother of the =fortunate boy. was present at. the time, and, knowing that the affair Was an acci- dent, desired that Grafton should not be apprehended. He was, however, arrested, but released on bail. NARROW ESCAPE OF A MAMAS PASIENGER STEAMFR. —There was a narrow escape from serious disaster en the Thames during a fog on Saturday evening. The General Steam Navigation Company's steamer Hawk was proceeding down the river for Hamburg, with about 50 passengers and a general cargo, when she was run into by a steam collier. The Hawk sustained such serious damage that she was obliged to be run ashore. The passengers landed in the steamer's boats. The Hawk subsequently almost entirely disappeared under water. Only one of the passengers sustained any injuries, but a stowaway, name unknown, on board the collier, was killed by the conion.

CHAINMAKERS' WA6V3 AOTTATIOV.—The Executive Committee of the,Chainmakers' As3ociation decided. on Saturday, at Cradtey Heath, to call a meeting of the employers and men with a view to a recognised scale of wages being established and a wages and concilation board formed. It Is stated that, although there is plenty of work at the present time, hundreds ef operatives were never in receipt of lower wages, and that, unless a sub- stantial advance is conceded, a general strike will be declared after Christmas. A number of employers have conceded an advance, and have thus appeased their workmen's agitation.

TUE POLITE LETTER-WRITERE.—The following letters have, says the Richmond and Twickenham Times, passed between Mr. Terry and a counsel learned in the law:— " Lincohi's Inn, Nov. —, 188—. Sir,—How can yon theatzivsla allow such a flagrant scandal as soldiers at Drury Lane? Really this prevents any respectable person from having anything to do with you people. Sarrister-at-la'.—Mr. Terry, Theatrical." To this Mr. Terry replied :—" Sir —I can only answer your ignorant and it:solent epistle by submitting the following conundrum :—flow is it possible that such an imbecile as you appear to be ever attained the position of barrister-at-law 7—Yours, E. TERRY." SWEATING IN !tartaric Wonx.—Of all forms of sweat- ing, that which pays artistic labour the lowest possible dribblet for weary days of patient and skilful technical application is the most revolting. Here are some of the prices quoted in a letter by Sophia Beale for hand-paint- ing t—u Ivory cards are paid 3s. and ss. a dozen; flower cards, 2s. a dozen; porcelain sla'ls, Is, 6d. to 3s. 6d. a dozen; small ivory tablets, Is. a dozen; menus, 3s. to /ss. a dozen; pin-cusitionn, 6d. a dozen; sachets, 6d. a down for painting, and 6d. a dozen for leaking them up. lly this vv6rk a woman clever with her brush may earn 12s. a week if she works ten or twelve hours a day."

SALVATION ARMY PETITION TO TITS HOME Snll-STARY. -At the "rouse of Commons on Monday, General Rooth presented to the Home Secretary a memorial from the Salvation Army askingi the Government to grant a sum of £15,000, or lend it free of interest, for the purpose of fitting no ten rescue homes for fallen women, and ten night shelters for houseloss women and men in various parts of the metropolis. The General made a statement to the effect that the Army.vras unable to provide suffi- cient accommodation for women in East London seek- ing shelter in consequence of the terrorism created by the recent murders. Mr. Matthews promised full con- sideration of the matter.

ATTEMPTED MURDER AT ALDERSHOT.—At an early hour on Sunday morning, a daring attempt to murder a woman was made in a cottage on the Redan Hill, Abler- shot. The man who made the attempt is a private sol- dier of the Commissariat and Transport Corps, named Cranstone. It appears that while he was in a room with the woman he took out of his pocket a razor, with which he said he was going to shave. The female's suspicions heing aroused, she endeavoured to get away, but he attacked her and tried to cut her throat. She, however, managed to escape from him, but not before she had re- ceived a severe cut. on the neck and another in the hands while protecting her throat. The man was arrested and taken to the police-station an hour after the occurrence. ,The motlie for the crime is said te be ieslousrv.

(3foortshine.) Lord Ranned-off proposes to pay an early visit to Chili. We would point out to his lordship that, when he gets there,•it is a very short trip, should he make up his mind, to go to Hong Kong. A case for a jury—Why, the jury bor. of course. Our representative at Berlin is to be made a peer. In other words, Malet is to have a new handle. Let us hope he will not lose his head over it.

What a fuss the Radicals are making because Lord Salisbury dropped the remark that Naoroji Sahib was a black man! Why don't they quote the context which •deprived the words of offence? But the joke of the thing is, that while the Homo Rulers protest that the whole black race has been insulted in the person of Naoroji. they are moving heaven and earth to show that Naoroji was not black at all. but white.:;

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 15, 1888.

WuAT can be done to assist the unemployed? That is a question which regularly arises in the ketropolis, when winter sets in; and various attempts have been made to furnish an answer but it cannot as yet be affirmed that anything - been said has bee said or done has proved wholly ' 44tisfactory. The question was again put to the LORD MAYOR at the Mansion House, on Tuesday, 111 six representatives of the unemployed who are
4ccuBtomed to assemble on Clerkenwell-green. They urged that the Government,"or the Vestries, Should find the people something to do. What they wanted was work—not charity. It is en easy

raatter to put men off by saying it is not the business of either the Government, .ar of the Vestries, to find citizens work at the expense of the taxpayers. It is certainly not the business of either of these bodies as they are at present con-

Atituted ; but, alter this has been said, the question 'still remains—What is to be done ? Anything or nothing? Assuming that there is a largo body of ttlen and women liho arise every morning willing : to work, but can find no work to do, we can scarcely Conceive of any condition more deplorable. It Aoems a poor outcome of our boa,sted civilization and thristianity that, with an accumulation of wealth elnounting to one hundred millions per year, there ahouldevery winter be 100,000 persons on the verge starvation because work is not t be had. This year there is an improvement trade;. :Z. there is a greater demand for skilled and I unskilled labour, and the unemployed should • be reduced to a minimum. There are some who Contend that, relatively to the whole body of: workers, there are really few people willing to toil who cannot find anything to d 4. They can- ' not, it is true, obtain such employment as they 'desire, but it is impossible for every sawyer to be 4 kip sawyer. The LORD MAYOR asked the depu- tation that waited upon him if they were willing to go to work at the price pail& by the Chelsea 'Vestry, two years ago, namely from fourpence to Oightpence per hour for eight hours work per day. .! The answer given was not satisfactory ; they Were not, they said, speaking for themselves, but as representatives of a larger body; and, besides, ' 'they could not take employment to which they Were probably unsuited." The latter becomes a ; knotty point. Have we got to this that the -demand of the employed is not only that work 611%11 be found for them, but work which in their 'opinion is suitable? We are afraid this is . 'Pushing the issue too far; the unemployed will damage an otherwise good case if they become over-nice as to the kind of work they are willing to undertake. Various experiments have been Made in London with a view to testing statements .as to willingness to take any kind of work which Would be the means of earning bread and -cheese. But they have for the most part proved failures. Of course, nothing was attempted on behalf of the notoriously intemperate °e criminal; but, even as to the rest, it was found that they fell off after a few days, or weeks. The employment was unsuitable or they found

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 15, 1888
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 15, 1888

they could go better elsewhere. All this has prodiiry discouraging to practical philanthro- pists; but, if they have failed once and again, shall they not again try ? We should like to see the 9xPeKiment made of an open workshop where men and women who had fallen into the ranks of the unemployed could find something to do. There Would soon be an outcry against an institution of this kind if it became a costly thing to the com- munity. But why should it ? Those who went• to this last resource would be willing to take the ordinary wage for work of the particular class for which they were best fitted; and with average management there ought to be an average result, which means that the workshops would pay their why, It trey were not a source of profit. We take no credit for a suggestion of this kind; it is Jomq Rusxm's idea. The only difference is that Rusiabi would make the workshops into training schools, and carry out his plan on a vast scale. That might come as the result of experiment; but in the first place it should be an experiment. Our point is that there ought to be something 'better than the Workhouse for the labourer or artisan who is "down on his luck"; and that something should be a Workshop.

We.usaranrox is moving slowly in the matter of candidates for the County Council. It does not appear that there are many persons who covet the distinction of representing a division of the borough and at the same time paying for the privelege by incurring such expenses as will immediately and hereafter be necessarily incurred. The Town Council—or, more strictly speaking, the members of the Town Council have taken upon themselves to consider who would make suitable representa- tives, for the three divisions into which the borough is divided, and at a special meeting, held on Monday evening, the choice fell upon Mr. JOHN FAntoLoroat, J.P.,and Councillors F. A. ROBERTS, and F. MONKS. It is not to be denied that these gentlemen would make excellent County Coun- cillors, and that they would fairly represent the ratepayers as a whole. They are all experienced and successful business men, who are, too, familiar with the management of public affairs. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH is a Conservative; Mr. ROBERTS is A Liberal; while Mr. Moxxs my be said to be sand- wiched between the two as a Liberal Unionist. There is a good deal said about nominations for the County Council being made on non-political lines; but we observe that this is usually done by Tories when they have a Tory to nominate, and wish to throw dust•in the eyes of Liberal electors. But the Conservative party have no need to show themselves -anxious in the case; there is - every reason to believe that they will have matters pretty much in their own hands; for the new act, having converted all the larg a towns into separate County Councils, boxes off a good deal of the Radicalism of the country.

Warrington has had the ill-luck, through its population being just short of 50,000, to be denied the title to became a Town Comity; but its boundaries are to be extended, and the question which instantly arises is, whether that extension shall be large enough 'to bring the population over 50,000. If the extensiOn which is proposed is to be so limited as not to extend the borough up to the line of the Ship Canal, at Latchford and Stockton Heath, it seems to us that—looking ahead—a grave mistake will be made. Already the growth of the town is largely in those quarters; and it is a matter of course to say that when the Ship Canal is completed the trend of population will, in all probability, be still more to the south and south-east. It is of moment to Warrington that it is affected by the Reports of the Boundary Commissioners, and that these Reports will be laid before 4'- 1 Couwils fox; )30t11 ---ro v 41,7 new Camay Laneashire and dheshirtl. The borough will 40 tio representativeg j.n. VIC Cheshire Council; but it fads With the electors to see to it that the three menlisikilifhich they send to the Lancashire Council know Whet they are about on this question; and, further, that they are pledged to the inhabitants. There has been some talk of nominating Mr. JOHN WHITE, for a &vision of Warrington, but, although he is in many respects an estimable gentleman, he is landlords' agent, and therefore not likely to be a free agent when it comes to giving a vote on the question of sufficiently extending the boundaries of the borough. It may be that one or more of the three gentlemen suggested by the Town Council will be found to have scruples in the matter; and that is a point which should be placed beyond doubt when they proceed, as we presume they will, to address the electors. The MAYOR has, it is understood, intimated his willingness, if requisitioned, to call a meeting cf the electors; but it seems to us that the Corpora- tion has gone quite far enough in its efforts to control the representation. Town Councillors, acting unofficially, have a perfect right to meet and say who would suitably represent them—just as any other body of men—Liberals, Tories, bakers, or butchers—have a right to meet and make such a selection as would best please them. The objection to a Town's Meethig is that no single meeting could, with authority, speak for the town. It is for the three divisions into which the borough is divided to act through the electorate, and deter- mine the representation. It is a good thing, espe- cially for candidates, to avoid expense, out, on the other hand, it will be good for the electors if there are meetings in every division. It should not be lost sight of that ft is a new Act which is being brought into operation, and its provisions are by no means familiar to the public. The County Councils will have large powers, and it is not unlikely that their powers will be greatly extended'. Speaking at Caine, on Tuesday, Lord Edmond Fitzmaurice said he "hoped to see the highway authority, the administration of the poor law, and even the super- vision of education transferred to these councils." These are large issues, and they ought to be well considered before steps are taken which may be irrevocable. There is the question, too, of licensing; it i by common consent held to be desirable that important powers as to this matter should be put into the hands of County Councils. It will not do for electors to leap in the dark; they should have candidates before them, and question them, if need be,not only as to present issues under the Act, but as to issues in the near future. We want men in the County Parliament as in the NationAl Par- liament who have made a study of the problems they will be called upon to solve—men who can give a reason for the faith that is in them, and who are actuated by a desire—not to serve their personal ends but to be of benefit to their kind.

-- The defunct Warrington Workmen's Club is shortly to be opened as a gymnasium. We wish the project every success. There is need for the development of muscle as well as mind, and the need will continue after this generation shall have passed away.

Russia is disposed to growl because we have acquired a trade footing in Persia. But Russia will profit too, if she will keep to her own side, and be quiet. It is no great thing, after all, to be on trading terms with" a country where there are only carriage roads for ninety-four miles and railways for about five." The Persians spend their time on rugs rather than roads. ,

The contributors to the Encyckpeediaßrittanica hare been feasting together by way of celebrating the completion of the ninth edition of that monu- mental work. It is especially interesting to lear that, while the eighth edition in 1860 amounted to 5,000 copies, the sale of the ninth edition already reaches between 40,000 and 50, 000 copies. This is surely a good sign ; " the more the merrier" say we.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, OA Monday, a lodging-house keeper was fined 40s. and costs for keeping his house in an insanitary condition. A butcher who had exposed' deceased meat for sale was fined on the same day ss. and costs only. Why is this thus ? Can it be that the magistrates made a mistake—that they meant £5 and costs? It would have \ been "more ger- mane to the matter."

The magistrates of Newton showed themselves considerate, on Saturday, in dismissing two boys, on payment of costs, who had been guilty of stealing bottles. It is as well to be lenient with juvenile first offenders, especially when the offence is of the minor kind. Appearance in court will have been no small punishment, and may make sneh an impression as will keep them from pilfering for the rest of their days.

There is a proposal to form a ring in the north- eastern section of England to secure a monopoly in flour. It is urged that it would effect such a saving, by dispensing with middlemen, and by grind- ing on a large scale, that a good profit would be assured without increasing the price of flour. That is the issue that will have to be watched; and woe be to him who places his hand between the mouths of the people and their food.

The test on the vacant land in Museum-street of the Imperial Fire Grenade Extinguisher was very successful on Thursday. People could scarcely believe their own eyes when they saw a mass of flame disappear as if by magic. Granted that the conditons wero favourable for the experiment, and making full allowance for this, it is still undeni- able that these grenades are what they claim to be— fire extinguishers of a most efficacious kind.

On Tuesday Mr. Justice Wills ordered the cat to be administered to a brutal young fellow named Atherton, who had been found guilty at the Liver- pool Assizes, of robbery with violence at Eccles- ton, near St. Helens. Experience shows that this form of punishment is 'more efficacious than long sentences. Reckless ruffians may be insen- sible to the degradation of prison life; but it has been found that they have a wholesome horror of the lash.

Mr. Goschen is being let off easy in the matter of the Van and Wheel Tax. It has been given up; but what provision is he making to raise the £700,000 which it had to bring in to the County Councils? None, so far as we can perceive. He shows himself "a poor stick," if he has no better idea of statesmanship than that. Try to fancy Mr. Gladstone landing himself into such a hole,' and neither resigning nor providing for the £700,000 But it Is impossible; it is boyond 4ne flight of fancy.

Lord,Clanricardre. is not to do as he likes. in the matter of evictions. By way of helping his tenants to "A Merry Christmas," he made arrangements to ittrn them out of house. and. harbour. But it seems there is a limit even. to the brutality of a Balfour. The Irish Sacretary has refused the forms of the Crown in this in- stance, and his lordsliiP is baffled and beaten back. It is te the credit of Mr. Balfour that he has' interfered; but, haying interfered, what becomes of his boast that he enforces the law, as he find/s- -it P Can it be that He has made up his mindtO assist in carrying out the Plan of Campaign

Mr. Quaritch is a man of rare books and ram prices, and he obtains both. He offers a Psalter• of the fifteenth century, for which he wants the sum of £5,220. It is described as "the grandest 0 • work ever produced by typography, and one of the rarest of the early monuments of printing." Granted, but for all that it is "a sin ad a shame" that so much money should be given for an old book. There is something rotten in the state,of England when money can be thrown away in this fashion whilst thousands cannot command the price of a meal or a bed: Oh, that a book should be so dear and flesh and'blood so cheap!

r MR. E. IMISON AND LORD R. CHURCHILL.—Lord Ran dolph Churchill in reply to a communication from Mr. 'ninon respecting the motion for the adjournment of the House on the Suakim question says that the case against the Suakim Expedition is so strong, and the line taken with respect to similar expeditions by the Tories when they were in opposition was so marked, that he felt very confident of receiving appreciable support from the ranks of the Ministerialists. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES CONSERVATIVE CM:M.—John Burns, a labourer, employed by Messrs. Sayce and Randle in the construction of the Conservative Club, met with a serious accident on Monday. He was stepping on to a plank on the scaffold kor the purpose of reaching a trowel, when the plank slipped from under him and he was precipitated below. He alighted upon a heap of bricks and timber and received serious injuries tothe body. He was conveyed to the Accident Hospital and is now under the care of Dr. McDpnnel. RUNCORN THEATRE ROYAL.—The exciting and romantic drama "Called Back" was performed at the Theatre Royal on the first three nights of the present week, and attracted large audiences. On Wednesday "The Unknown" was placed on the stage, and will be repeated this (Saturday) evening. The various characters are strongly repreSented. Next week Mrs. Edward Saker, formerly lessee and manageress of the Alexandra Theatre, Liverpool, will fulfil an engagement at the theatre, and it is hoped th:it lovers of the drama will assemble in large nunthers to welcome this talented lady. She will appear as Marie in the drama " The Woman of the People." It is probable that Mrs. Saker will shortly again undertake the management of a Liverpool theatre. ROMAN CATHOL!C PROGRESS IN WIDNES.—The annual report of the Liverpool Diocesan Roman Catholic Mission Fund was reed on Sunday in all the churches of the Roman Catholic diocese by the direction of Bishop O'Reilly, who, in the course of his statement, says : You (the Catholic congregations) will gladly listento a statement of what has been done since we last addressed you upon this subject. The town of Widnes, which, withinthe memory of living men, was marked on the hanks of the river Mersey by a ferry-house, has grown Into a town of laree dimensions. A large industry was established there, and the few Catholics who then resided there had, in order to hear mass, to journey to the church nearest to them, that a Appleton. About 25 years ago a new mission was established. 'File beginning was indeed humble, but from that humble beginning great fruit resulted. A fine church was built, which at the time was judged to be too large for any possible requirement. Larae schools were also erected. The church was found not to be at all too spacious, and the -schools have at various times been largely added to, and even when thus enlarged it was found to be necessary to buildother schools inn different part of the town. Then the church was found to be too small and too far removed for the convenience of the peop!e, and the self- sacrificing pastor would give himself no rest till he caused to be built art additional church, larger than the parent church alongside the schools, over which. in the midst of numerous difficulties, he had watched for many years. The report also details the progressof Catholicism in Preston, Liverpool, Seaforth, and Maehull. MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, WIDNES.—LI the vestry of this place of worship, a sale of work was held on Thursday afternoon .and evening. The members of the ladies' sewing class had gathered together a large assortment of fancy needlework and other articles, which were displayed on two stalls. There was also a refreshment stall. The ladies who presided were Mrs. Halsall, Mrs. Chapman, Mrs. Deming Mrs. Seepherd, Mrs. Knowles, Mrs. Scott, Mrs. Guise, Miss Barton, and Mrs. Lewis (secretary). There was a good company present at the opening ceremony, and included the Rees. It. G. Hughes (pastor), T. Law, E. Hall, D. Davies, and H. Owen, and Major Brunner. After devotional exer- cises, Mr. Hughes mentioned that the object of the sale was to raise £5O towards the current expenses of the year. Wales, he said, did not indulge in bazaars or sales of work, but in England people were not so religiously inclined as those of Scotland and Wales, and hence they werea, necessity. The ministers of the town worked very well considering these difficulties, and their difficulties would be much greater than they were had not it been for the cordial suppoet which had been given to every denomination by the manufacturers. Although the majority of the manuFacturers did not live in the town, they were thoroughly in sympathy ,with and were not backward in helping the intellectual, moral, and spiritual welfare of the inhabitants. (Applause.) Major Brunner then addressed those pre- sent, and remarleel that he did not think that it had 'been alnico': at any time to raise money for good object n Viridnea. (Hear, hear.) He did not think that it had been altogether a good thing, because these gentlemen had given so generously that others might have, to some extent, forgotten their reeponsibilitios. Those who had most money probably ought to give it, but he suggested that when next they were called upon to give largely, they should inquire what the people who wore asking had done for themselves. DEATH OF A GREAT COTTON KING.—Mr. John Rylands, head of the great firm of John Rylands and Co., Limited, Manchester, justly famed as the monarchs of the cotton industry of England died on Tuesday morning. The firm had a very modest beginning in 1819, and at first John Ryles& was accustomed to travel through the country on horse-back, with his samples, soliciting orders. The concern prospered enormously, and underwent gigantic developments. John Rylands being eventually as the head of it. Later on it was converted into a limited liability company, capital two roirliorre, with a 'million and , a hair paid up. The, transactions of the company amounted to millions a year. The weight of out- put is caleida,ted at from =MO to 30,000 tons, and the company's imports of cotton worth £25t1000 ammully. The company hzove-seventeen mills and factories,, and employ no fewer than 12,000 hands. The late. Mr. Rylands was a munificient supporter of the liTaneheaterShip Canal. When one of She Select Cbmmittee of the Muse of Commons required' evidence to show that the bill worid be finaneiaily supported by Lancashire merchants, Mr. Ryan& offered to tam- .C 50,000 word of shares. A BINDOSTANEE GIRL-WIDOW AtiT Sr. HELENS.— ,On Friday, at the St. Helens Town Hall, Mary Ann Hyde, who, in appearance, was like a child, but who wore a wedding ring, was charged with begging oat the previous evening—lnspector Goodall, who, it appears, is a linguist, by talking to, the girl in her native tong' ue ascertained that she came from Surat. in the Bombay Presidency. She had upon her a begging letter, which had been undoubtedly written by some uneducated English person. It was as follows:—" Ladies and Geistiemen,—l don't belong to this country. lam a native of Bombay, in India. / was married very young, at the age of 13, that being the custom of my country. Now I am twenty-two; my husband being a soldier in the 83 rigiment, but now he is ded. I apply to you for a little assistance. I am Yours, Humble Servant, MB& Ilvon."—Chief Constable Wood stated that the prisoner was apprehended at eleven o'clock the previous night. She was going from shop to shop N and when assist- ance was refused she would walk into the kitchen and use bad language.—Mr. Sinclair: Where are you going?—Prisoner clasped her hands and assumed an attitude of prayer, and cried out: " Me make to Liverpool; me not do it any more, sir."—Mr. Sin- : You will go out of the town will you?—Pri- soner: Oh, yes, me not stop.—Mr. Sinclair: Let her go then.—The prisoner then made a rush towards the door leading to the cells, the way in which she had been brought into court. On being told that that was the wrong way, she looked round t the room, and seeing there was only one more door, ' she bolted towards it as quickly as her legs would carry her, amid loud laughter.

ALLEGED OUTRAGE CA A GIRL NEAR' WIDNES.—At Widnes Pbtty Sessions on Thursday, Lloyd Jones, 19 years of age,.of Limelalmla.ne, Halewood, vras Jamught up to answer a charge of' indecently assaulting Mary Ford, 16 years of age, who. lives vrith her parents at 16, Harrison-st.,, Flalebank. The complainant, a young lady who looked much older than her years, said that on Sunday night she was returning home after having obtained same milk at a farm house, when she was met by the prisoner and anothes-young man named William Houghton. The prisoner bade her "the time of the night." adid not answer, and he put his left arm around her shoulders and forced her against the rails that fenced the footpath, and acted indecently towards her. He had her in such a position that she could not resist, and' she could not shout. She informed her mother of his conduct, and warrant was obtained for his apprehension.—The prisoner was remanded until Monday next so that he could be professionally defended. He was liberated On bail. BANKRUPTCY OF A WIDNES" rITBLICAN.—On Thursday the case of Henry Turner came before Mr. Registrar Bellringer at Liverpool Bankruptcy Court. The debtor had been a publican at Widnes, where he occupied the Wellington Hotel up to a recent date. Since then he had been manager of a public-house in Sr. Anne-st., Liverpool. The statement of affairs showed liabilities £613, and no assets. In examination by the official receiver, the debtor said he was receiving 30s. a week in his present situation, and was willing to pay 108. a week towuds the liquidation of his debts. it appeared that the house the debtor had occupied at Widnes Was "tied "to a firm of brewers for beer, and he attributed his failure partly to bad trade and competition, and partly to the high price he had to I pay for his beer, viz., 425. a barrel net, instead of 425. with a large discount. it transpired during the exam- ination that the debtor had called a meeting of his creditors, at which he made the same offer of 10s. a week, and that a firm of accountants in Liverpool had drawn up a deed providing for this, for which they charged six guineas. The registrar advised these accountants to be careful as to such matters, for there was such a thing in existence as the Solicitors' Act. He adjourned the examination to the 17th January.
