Mr. Thomas Whittaker, of the Stanley Arms, Lugs- dale-road, wrote on the 14th November complaining that owing to the deficiency in the gas engineer's department he was without gas on Monday evening last from 7 o'clock p.m. toll o'clock a.m. next day. This had been a great annoyance to him for trade purposes, many curomers calling for a cup of coffee before going to business. Nevertheless he did think the gas engineer ought at least to use civility. After closing his house he went to Mr. Carr's residence and explained the circumstances, and asked him what he, should do to have the gas alight for the morning, and the only answer he got was" Do what the devil you like." Considering that Mr. Carr was receiv- ing the salary he did, from the pockets of the ratepayers of Widnes he thought his conduct was censurable. Mr. Gasket' moved that the letter lie on the table. The gas failed about seven o'clock in the evening, and about one o'clock in the morning Whittaker appeared at Mr. Saddler's h use and called him out of bed. He then went to Mr. Carr's between one and two o'clock, awoke him from his bed, and expected him to get up and start the men at once at the street to discover what was wrong. Mr. Carr argued with the man from the bed- room window, but Whittaker refused to go away with- out " satisfaction." The matter was attended to as soon as the men came to work in the morning ; it was several hours work, and work that could not be possibly under- taken at night. If members of the Board and all the officials were to be called up at all hours of the night by anyone who had a complaint of that sort to make, it would be unbearable.—Mr. lieyes seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.

div.head: HOARD AND SUNDAY CLOSING.
div.p: THE HOARD AND SUNDAY CLOSING.

Mr. J. Reay, of 4 Dickson-street, wrote that a peti- tion so reasonable and yet withal of Slierl importance to Widnes as that for Sunday closing of public-houses, should have been treated with such levity at the. last Board meeting, would be matter for regret to many if Rot all of those who had the welfare of the community and the leve of their fellows at heart. In face of all the evidence that could easily be produced showing how terrible were the curses which followed in the wake of Sunday drinking, and on the other hand how great the blessings which accrued from Sunday abstinence, then the wonder was that the ' petition did not receive the sanction even of those gentlemen whom they knew from best experience were not friends of the Sunday closing movement. That it should have been rejected on political grounds made it the more to be regretted when they remembered that politicians of all Shades, and in many instances publicans themselves, were favourable to the movement. But he begged respectfully to submit that this was not a political matter, but a matter purely of right or wrong -, therefore he trusted that gentlemen constituting the Board weuld see their way clear still to take action in the matter, and in such a way as to do honour to themselves and the town whose interests, for the time being, were placed in their keeping,.—The Chairman said at the last meeting this matter was con- sidered to, be outside the province of the Board. He thought the former action of the Board was quite a sufficient reply to the letter.—Mr. Carey said it was not a question whether the members of the Board sympa- thised with Sunday closing or not, but simply whether they were appointed to take cognizance of and deal with such a matter. The Board said they were not.

div.head: GAR AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAR AND WATER COMMITTEE.

The Engineer reported that the water had now fallen below the suction of the pumps of the engines Virginia and Mary at Stock's Well, so that as a duplicate source of supply they were practically useless. If any serious accident should occur to the "Gossage" Engine, so as to prevent it working for any considerable period, some difficulty might be experienced in maintaining a sufficient supply.. It was, therefore, necessary that a scheme for providing a duplicate supply should receive the Com- mittee's early attention. The mean rainfall for the past month was 4.565 inches. The water in stock was 7,151, 811 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 18-61 candles.—The minutes , were passed on the motion of Mr, Gaskell.

div.head: ALLEGED EPIDEHIC OF FEVER.
div.p: THE ALLEGED EPIDEHIC OF FEVER.

Dr. Cooper, the medical officer of Health, reported that during November there were 92 births and 39 deaths, being at the respective rates of 36.8 and 15.6 per 1,000. The deaths included 13 children under one year and 12 children between one and five years. Zrnetic disease caused 7 deaths.—Mr. Carey said there was an impres- ion abroad that there NW a good deal of illness in the district,but the death rate did not indicate such a state of affairs. The Medical Officerinformedhim in a letter that Ithe scarlet fever which was prevalent last month was of a mild type and there were very few eases at present. There was no person suffering from typhoid or typhus fever, i except those at present n the hospital,and they were con- valescent. Dir. Carey .said, there was no doubt a great ant of cleanliness It; epidemic disease, especiallvs.he tint; andlntrll.,rn d to o remove this when the Board took the nightsoll removal into their own hands. The Health Committeo were about to take steps to• prevent the overcrowding that occurred in many cottages and were also going to deal strictly with the question of pigs in backyards.—Dr. O'Keeffe said there was nothing like an epidemic in Widnes and never bad been. The report that Widnes was a fever stricken town was calculated to prevent people visi ing the town and to drive people out. If at any future time there should be a change in the govern- ment of the town he should advocate the compulsory Inotification of infectious disease. (Rear, hear.)—The Chairman said if he were a young married man coming to the town it would not be the death-rate, but the birth-rate, that would frighten him. (Laughter.)

div.head: ALKALI WASTE NUISAkCII.
div.p: ALKALI WASTE NUISAkCII.

• Mr. Thomas Sadler wrote stating that alkali waste was being laid nearer to Violet-st. than he understood was agreed to, and the tenants were complaining of the stench from it.—Mr. Carey explained that the Cheshire Lines Railway Company were making a cartway approach to the new goods depot, and they Were making a retaining wall of alkali waste. The waste would be well laid with common salt, for waste laid ire that way did not smell That was his experience.—Mr. Heyes said they had the evidence of tenants that it did, and he moved that notice be drawn to the agreement entered into that no alkali waste should be deposited within WM yards of any dwelling, and that the company be asked to make the road of some othermaterial.—Mr. Houghton seennded the motion.—Mr. Gaskell remarked that it would not be just to the ratepayers to allow a nuisance to be pfaced at their doom in order to save interested persons a few pounds.—Themotion was carried.

POLICE AND` PUBLICANS AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. John Brunelrit and Mr. G. L. Davies,. at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, James, Ditchfield, landlord of the Royal Hotel, was sum- moned for 14aving en the Ist December permitted drunkenness to take place on his premises, and also for supplying! drink to a drunken person.—Mr. Jenkins, of Warrington, defended. Inspector O'Donnell deposed that about a quarter past ten on .the night of the ffrst inst., he visited the Royal ' ,Hotel, and in a little "snug" he found a man very drunk and asleept. He had a half-pint pot half 'filled with ale before him. He tried to rouse the man, but could not do so, and it was not until Mr. White, the manager of the house held the man's . nose and shook him that he awoke. The man gave the name of George Reader and he afterwards found that he was a navvy from the neighbolnikood of Ellesmere Port. He told Mr. White he should be ebliged te report the circumstance,. and the latter replied "I will take him to a doctor; don't think there is much the matter with him." The man drank a portion of the beer in his presence.—By Mr. Jenkins: He did not remember the man deny that he, was drunk: and s‘si that probably he might be from his (the inspector's) point of view. He did ask the man how he spelt his name, but he did nek remember the man saying that if he were fit for his position, he ought to be able to spell his name.—Mr. Jenkins: To every question I ask, it is "I cannot remember," or you pause. From a trained man like yourself, Inspector, we expect a straight answer.—ln reply to further questions; the Inspector said the man stood up at the request ot White. He did not stand firm and steady.—P.S. Woolley gave corroborative testimony. The man was certainly drunk. —P.C. Burne and Sergeant Gosling also gave evidence. The latter officer declined to say whether he had ever expressed to another person that this man was not drunk.—Mr. Jenkins said the Inspector and other officers had given their evidence very fairly indeed. It was quite impossible for public officers to be perfect or immaculate, in the discharge of , their duties, and it was equally difficult for licensed victuallers to steer clear of the many dangers, temPta- tions andrisks by which their business was surrounded. , It was extremely difficult for a publican at times to judge when a man who entered, hia laouse, was tipsy.

He contended that there was a doubt in this case, and that it must be proved that there was some guilty knowledge, on the part of the defendant, of the fact that intoxicants were being supplied to a man who had had enough. He called Thomas White the manager of the hotel, Wm. Brown, an assistant, and Henry Williams, tailor of Grosvenor-st. who all stated that the man was sober. He entered the house at the bar, and was served with a pint of beer. He after- wards carried his beer across the bar into the snug, and he walked upright and steady. After the officer had been at the house, White took the man across to the Police Station for the purpose of confronting him with the superintendent, but the latter was not at home. He should have supplied the man with another glass of beer while the inspector was there had he asked tor one. He had heard that the man was afterwards apprehended for being drunk in the street.—Mr. Brundrit said the Bench consider id the police had done their duty, but there was a doubt in the case, and the defendant would be dis- missed.

ST. AMBRQSE CHURCH BAZAAR, WIDNES. In aid of the organ and vestry fund of St. Ambrose Church, Halton View, a bazaar was com- menced in Lacey-st. schoolroom on Wednesday riftein on. Last week a handsome organ which had been constructed at a cost of .£450 was opened in the church, and, as the organ chamber had been previ- , ously used as a vestry, an additional room is there- fore rendered necessary. Messrs. Brown and Backhouse, of Liverpool, are at present engaged in the erection of a new vestry on the south side of the chancel, the external appearance harmonizing with the architecture of the main building. The total cost of the organ and building is about £B5O. Towards this sum about .£450 has been obtained, or promised, of which Mr. George Pilking- ton, J.P., and Mr. Leonard Pilkington each gener- ously contributed £lOO. A large and fashionable company assembled at the bazaar on Wednesday, when the opening ceremony wat performed by Mr. G. Pilking- ton. After a brief speech from the Rev. G. He hoped that the bazaar would be an unqualified success, and that the amount acquired would be realized. (Applause.) He then declared the bazaar open.—Mr. J. Brock said they were much indebted to Mr. Pilkington- and his brother for the interest they had ta.ken in the scheme; and the liberal way in which they had supported it. The Bible Class provided dissolving views by a powerful magic lantern. The receipt of the first clay'a sale amounted to about £2OO.

The bazaar was continued on Thursday, when Mr. E. Carey performed the opening ceremony, and in his speech he entered into a defence of bazaars. ill- natured persons said that at bazaars proceedings were tolerated that would not be permitted elsewhere, but that was not his experience, Bazaars were extremely useful institutions, and raised a lot of money for praiseworthy objects, which could not perhaps be obtained in any other way, besides giving the members of the congregation an opportunity of becsming better acquainted with each other. He congratulated the con- gregation of St. Ambrose upon the possession of a minister who had his heart in his work, and expressed his pleasure at being amongst old friends. He hoped the success of the previous day alight be continued and increased, and declared the bazaar open.—Mr. ;Carey was cordially thanked for his services, on the motion of Mr. Johnson, seconded by Mr. Brock.

Before Mr. Justice Wills on Thursday, the following cases were heard:—

Lawrence Mulroy (35), labourer, was found guilty of having, at Widnes, on the 28th October, unlawfully wounded Thomas M'Cann during a fight. Primmer was sentenced to four months' imprisonment, with hard labour.

He did not like to send them to I. frw their first offence . , iutt so, having warned them as to their future conduct, bound them over to come up for sentence when called upon.

BRCTAL ATTACK ON AN OM WOMAN AT WIDNES. John Killalea (20), labourer, was indicated forhaving, on July 28th, at Widnes, indicted grievous bodily harm upon Bridget Glynn, an old woman of 63. Mr. Tobin prosecuted, and said the case was one of singular bru- tality. On the day in question she was standing :at her own house door, when the prisoner, who was drunk, went up to her, and without any provocation knocked her down. The old woman got up, and ran into the house, locking the door behind her. Prisoner went to one of the windows and broke it open, and threw a bucket of cold water over Glynn. Be afterwards got through the window, and chased the old woman all round the house, catching her in the front room, where he beat her most brutally with a wooden stool, with which he knocked her down. She was l:adly injured, her head and body being fearfully bruised, and one of her ribs broken.—Prisoner was found guilty, and having been already four months in prison, he was sentenced to two months with hard labour.—Prisoner: Thank you, my lord, I'll never take drink any more.—His Lordship: Well, see that you don't, or you will be getting yourself into even worse trouble.

div.head: THREAT TO MURDER.
div.p: THREAT TO MURDER.

Patrick Mrabe, age 22, described as a fish dealer, was charged with baying done grievous bodily harm to John Kinsella, on the 10th October, at Widnes. Mr. Cooper prosecuted. and the prisoner was defended by Mr. Sefear. The prosecutor, it seemed, was an elderly and weakly man. On the night of the date in question, prisoner pushed open the door of prosecutoesehouse; and shouted "Whereis the old swine ?I have come to murder him." Prisoner then seized hold of the man by the throat, kicked hint several times in the face, and pre- vented him getting out of the house. Prisoner also struck prosecutor's daughter in the face several times because she tried to protect her father. Wheh prisoner had got Kinsella into the street, he kicked him in the groin, dragged him into the gutter, and jumped upon him, rendering him insensible. For several days Kin- sells was very ill, his spine having been injured.—For the defence it was denied that the prisoner had jumped upon Kinsella, or inflicted grievous bodily harm. Prisoner simply entered the house to take away his female cousin, he fearing that she was in a house of ill- flame.—The jury found the prisoner guilty.—His Lord- ship said that the prisoner had Mused a man not half his size and twice his age. It was the worst case of violence that had been tried at these assizes. Prisoner must go to jail for twelve months.—When leaving the deck, prisoner said "I can do it on my head." "ESCAPED' EY THE SKIN or TREIE TNETH." William 'rayloe„Henry Taylor, James Worrell, and James Whyke, young men, were indicted for having, on October 14, at Hale, maliciously and feloniously wounded Thomas Burke, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. Mr. M'Connell prosecuted, and, Mr. Swift defended.. The case against the Taylors was taken first, and the-evidenee showed that they assaulted Burke in a lane at Hale, William Taylor using, a, stick and Henry Taylor his fists. They were foiled guilty of unlawfully wounding. His lordship put William Taylor back until the nest day, so that he might consider how to deal with him; and Henry Taylor was allowed out, after being bound over to come up for sentence when called upon—On the case against Worralt and Whyke coming up his lordship pointed out that from the evidence which had already been given.. these two pri- soners did not come on the scene until the wounding was over. No doubt the prisoners had also assaulted Burke, but they were not indicted:. for assault. Con- sequently he must direct the jury to find Worrell and Whyke not guilty of wounding.—The jury having returned a verdict to that effect, his lordship, addressing the prisoners, said, "You have got off by the skin of your teeth, because you are charged with something which does not properly describe what you have done. You might be again brought up for the assault, but I don't recommend that course, as you have already been in prison far two months. This is what comes of spend- ing your Sunday evenings in public-houses, and getting half-seas over. Let this be a warning to you." The prisoners were then liberated,

div.head: WESLEYAN MISSIONARY ANNIVER, _
div.p: WESLEYAN MISSIONARY ANNIVER- , _
SARY.

----- • On Sunday anniversary services in connection with the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society were held at Wesley Chapel, Bewsey-road, Warrington. The pulpit was occupied in the morning. by the superintendent of the circuit, the Rev. E. Young, and in the evening by the Rev. E. H. Jackson. There were good congregations. The annual meet- leg was held on Monday evening, under the presi- dency of Mr. J. B. Isaac. Supporting the Chair- man on the platform were the Rev, G. E. Young (Manchester), Rev. G. Young, Rev. W. Brookes, Rev. E. H. Jackson, Mr. J. 'Shaw Green, and' Mr. John Bennett.—The Rev. W. Brookes (secretary) submitted a report in which it was mentioned that towards last year's income of the society Warrington contributed £Bl ' 161.—The Chairman reinaltked that I signs were not wanting that the prospects of the society were brighter and more hopeful than they were twelve menths ago. His hearers knew that there had been a decrease in the society's income, and that had occurred just at a time when the expenditure had been a little in excess of the average, thereby creating a deficiency of about £16,000. Thet debt had given rise to a good deal of discussion and criticism of the opera- tions and policy of the society-. If criticism was I prompted merel,;lay a spirit of fault finding, with no I higher motive than to run missionary effort down, such a course would be unjust and unfair. But if, on the other hand, that discussion and criticism had po- teeded from a sincere desire to promote its welfare, and to seeit flourish and prosper, then he thought in the end discussion would do good. (Hear, hear.) It had done good in the present case. The Wesleyan Missionary Society and the great missionary cause was more popular with Methodist people to-day than it was some time ago ; and the secretaries would be none the less respected and esteemed than they were before the discussion arose. The Wesleyan Missionary Society had moo on the mission field who were so zealous and earnest that before they would retreat in face of the enemy they would die, (Applause.) The only thing which would cause a real earnest devoted missionary to fall back was a word from the Mission House, and the authorities at the Mission House would not send that word if the Methodists of Warrington and throughout the country would do their duty. (Applause.) They needed to be up and doing. Those of his hearers who had been brought up in Warrington would remember—and especi- ally those who were present at Pr. Smith's funeral on Saturday—that someone was needed to step in his place and carry on the work. (Hear, hear.) If they could only get some of the spirit which animated , him who was laid, in the grave on Saturday, that meeting, aye, tho Warrington circuit, would be all in a blaze. (Applause.) —Brief addresses having been delivered by the circuit ministers, the Rev. G. E. Cutting, who was present, gave an address at the request ot the chairman. He said the successes of the Wesleyan and all other Missionary Societies had been successes of the 19th century. He had to chide himself, and no doubt his hearers had to chide themselves, for lack of devotion to that. work. (Hear. hear.) The people of this country spent £130,000,000 in intoxicating drink every year, and only 21,500.000 in mission work. That was the sort of devotion of whjch they were short. ,Just reverse ' those figures, and suppose that oily £1,500,000 went in drink—worse, than wasted even then—and £130,000,000 going to spread Christ's truth abroad. What immense strides mission work would make then I (Hear, hear.) Go with him a moment to France. He confessed to a recent fascination concerning European nations. France was a profoundly interesting country nominally Roman Catholic, actually atheistic. Supposing £130,000,000 were given by the people of this Country for the spread of the Lord's I work in France, how the cause would prosper!. The 1 society had some workers there now, but what sort I of a light was it? Could any but God convert ? Could any but the Holy spirit renew and save ? Could any physician but Jesus heal the wounds of sin ? Well, then, if there had been conversions in Paris, God was there; and if God was there he could not, would not, and dare not despair. (Applause.) It was morn- ing twilight in Italy. The Pope would like to have back his temporal power and his Italian territory, but he would never get them. (Hear, hear.) China, Burmah, and other countries were ready for the clear light, for there were already lights in thAiarkness. Some.of those children of the night had already stars of hope—morn- ing stars whose feeble lustre might ere this have guided some of them to heaven, but whose insufficient beams would shortly melt into the opening close of the Gospel day. (Applause.)—On the motion of Mr. John Bennett, seconded by Mr. John Hayward, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the Chairman and Mr. Cutting for their services and addresses; and the meeting closed with the Doxology and Benediction.
A COMPLAINT AGAINST INSPECTOR O'DONNELL, OF RUNCORN.„ THE SOLICITOR AND THE CHIEF CONSTABLE.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Mon—clay, Mr. W. 11. Linaker, solicitor, made a complaint before the sitting magistrates (Mr. J. Brundrit• and Mr. G. L. Davies), with regard to the coquet of Mr. Inspector O'Donnell. The following letter will show the ground of the complaint : • " 58, lligh-street, Runcorn, 5, November, 1888. Sir,—We were consulted on Monday last by Mr. Thomas Harrison, if licensed victualler in this town and also a farmer, as to the conduct of Inspector O'Donnell on Saturday the 10th instant. Mr. Harrison as well as being a licensed victualler, is a tenant of a farm belonging to the Trustees of the Duke of Bridge- water. From time to time people in going from Runcorn to Weston Point have crossed a field in his occupation as a short cut from one place to the other. On the dayin question, the inspector went through the farm yard and saw a notice hoard stating "No Road." He asked a man in Harrisen's employ whether there was a publio road across the field or not. The man said " no," and pointed out the road by which he ought to go. The inspector, however, proceeded to cross the field. The man seeing this called the attention of Mr. Harrison's son to what was going on, and the latter called after the inspector and went up to him and told him that he was trespassing. In spite of this, the inspector declited to turn back and.got over the fence at the other end of the field. On the evening of the same day, the inspector in company wit's a policeman entered Mr. Harrison's house and saw two men in the vaults. Only one man had been served with refreshments, the other man only just having entered the vaults. A eon of Mr. Harrison was in charge of • the vaults at the time. Mr.., Harrison hearing some conversation went himself into the vaults, and saw the inspector and policeman. The inspector asked him to whom the beer on the table belonged. Harrison told him and stated also that he had not seen the other man till then and he could not have been served, and the inspec- tor told him he did not believe him. After looking through the house and finding nothing wrong, the inspector and policeman were leaving the house and Mr. Harrison callel the former back and said (pointing to the man who had last ODNIO in) "The man has not been served here, and if you think him drunk will you ask your officer to put him out ?" The inspector turned back into the valets again and said to Mr. Harrison, "You had better he careful or I'll have you before long." Mr. Harrison is very indignant at the conduct of the inspector, and as before stated consulted us on Mon- day. We at once saw the Clerk to the Justices with a view of bringing tho matter before the Bench next Monday. Mr. Ashton, at the end of our interview, promised to give our communication his consideration. We saw him yesterday and he informed us that he did not see in what form we 'could bring the matter before the Bench, and referred us td you. The above facti can be corroborated on oath, and we ask your attention to them with a view to holding an inquiry for taking evidence.—We are, Sir, your onedient servants, LINAKKR AND LINAKER. Colonel Hamersley, Chief Constable, Chester." Mr. Linaker said on the 27th November he received a very unsatisfactory reply to that communication, accepting everything from- Inspector O'Donnell and , ignoring every word that Harrison, who was, a highly respectable man, and had not the slightest spot upon his ' character, had said. The letter read as follows : " Referring to your letter of the 15th hist as to two com- plaints made by Mr. Harrison against Inspector O'Donnell, I have seen the Inspector on the Isubject. He acknowledges that he did trepass, but committed no damage whatever to Mr. Harrison's property; but simply crossed a field and jumped a hedge at the end of it, into the road. However the Inspector will net repeat his/ action In this matter. ' As to the second part of your letter,' Inspector O'Donnell denies that lie ever threatened Mr. Harrison iu the way alleged, or in any other way, when he visited the houso in question. I see no I reason to hold an inquiry into the matter." ' Here, said Mr. Linaker was an allegation which could not be trumped up, and he thought the Chief Constable should treat the ratepayers of the county, with some little respect, and not take the statement of a man like O'Donnell without inquiry. He did not ask the Bench to express any opinion. The Chief Constable (who was present on the Bench) said he made inquiry; he did not I think anything further necessary. Mr. Linaker said the 1 ratepayers of the couuty ought to be treated -with proper respect, and he objected to the Chief Constable making remarks from the Bench. The Chief Constable: You must like it or not if I have any remarks to make. Mr. Linaker: You have no locus standi in this court. The Chief Constable: Upon this subject, I have as much ocus statdi as you. It is not a proper subject to be brought before the Court. Mr. Linaker: I shall not leave it entirely to your sole jurisdiction. The ordinary business of the Court was then °proceeded with, the magistrates making no comment.

WELEBACH Lieut.—A new method of lighting by gas, the inVention of Dr. Carl Auer von Welsbach, is now being exhibited by the Incandescent Gaslight Co., Limited, Guardian Building, Cross-st., Manchester. The gas when burnt under this system gives off neither carbon nor sulphur and com- paratively little heat, and it is estimated that a saving oLSO per cent. is effected in consumption, with greatly superior illuminating to ewer. WARRINGTON WRITH STAR T. lar..Am WANDRINIRS.— Played on the ground of the former and resulted in a draw ; score: White Star trios 4 minors ; Wanderers, 2 tries 2 minors.
WPAITaII 18T Y. WEDNRS Justons.—This match was played at Widnes on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the home team by 1 goal, 2 tries, and 6 minors to 2 tries and 1 minor,
LATCHFORD Ho 11:1113Te Y. W. BOOTIE'S TRAIL—This match was played at Latchford on. Saturday, the home team being strongly represented. Scores :—Latchford, one minor; W. Booth's team, one minor. _

DZKINFIRLD RRI, STAR Y. RUNCORN PAMEIR CRIIRCR EXOlll.6iOUS.—The match was played on the ground of the former, and resulted in a win for Excelsior% byl try, 4 minors, to six minors. Borrows gaining the try, but Hitchmough failing to convert it into a goal. Minshull, Harrison, and Dutton played well for the home team. Hitchmougb, Lockett, Smitham, Borrows, and Broady, were best for the opposite team.

RUNCORN ?Will iiI.UBS V. RUNCORN PRIM WANDERNRS. —These teams met on theground of the former on Satur- day. Throughout the game, which was very fast, the home team. found their opponents plenty to do, and in less than ten minutes Taylor had scored the first try. When half-time arrived the score was—Blues, 1 goal, 1 try, and 6 minors to nil. In the second half the home team again had matters their own way. Taylor and Hassell secured tries, from one of which Inman landed a goal. The final score stood—Blues, 2 goals, 3 tries, and twelve minors to nil.

WYCLIFFII 2ND T. ST. ELTEllel.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Sathrday.. The visitors' captain kicked off, and the play was of a gi've- and-take nature until Blackmore secured a fair catch in the home 25, from which he dropped a goal. This was the only major point scored in the first-half, St. Elphin's crossing over a goal to the good. The second half was keenly contested, both sides striving hard to score, and it was not until live minutes from time that Myles ran in a try for St. Elphin's, from which Butter- worth kicked a goal, the score finally reading—Bt. Elphin's, 2 goals, 4 minors ; Wycliffe, 1 minor.

• VVIDNItS' ASPITIL.—These teams met on the Lower- house-lane ground, Widnes, on Saturday, and the con- test was witnessed by a large number of spectators. Aspull were minus a number of their prominent men, amongst them being Hesketh, Haydock, Jackson, Cart- wright,Birchall,John and James Lindsay, and eventually played fourteen men. The home team played up the slope at the commencement, and a minor each was added. Samuels for Aspull succeeded in gaining the first try, which Morris was equally successfain converting into a goal. Parkinson did some commendable running for the homesters, and shortly after Barber rushed up to the line and managed to ground the ball, thus securing for the chemicals their first try amid some applause. Plumpton took the place kick with success. The work done by Farrell and Clarke was worth noting. Howard's play made him appear somewhat conspicuous, as his smart tactics were of a gratifying character. J. Smitiji at length obtained a try, from which Plumpton landed another goal, after which half-time was called, the score standing—Widnes, 2 goals. 2 minors, to Asyut!, 1 goal, 2 minors. In the second half the game was somewhat uninteresting, being rather slow. From a free kick near the home line Morris made a futile attempt at goal ; then Clarke did a neat run, from which l'arltia.son got over the boundary and scored :another try, and Plump- ton succeeded in registering the major point. The home team kept up a continual pressure, Plumpton getting over the line, but his appeal for a try was not allowed. Final score :—Widaes, 3 goals, 3 minors; Aspull, I goal, 3 minors. ST. liners v. LANCASTInt.—Tho St. Helens fifteen visited Lancaster on Saturday, but they had only a weak team. The following were the players: St. Helens.—Full back, T. C. Lucas; three-quarter backs, W. Lund, E. Foreman and H. Garrard; half backs, W. Cross and G. E. Summers; forwards, A. Borthwick (captain), Graham, McLaus,rhlan, Ellison, Twist, Wilson, Slater. Huyton and Brownbill. Lancaster.—Full back, Sandland ; three-quarter backs, Moscrop, Hartley, and Lambert ; half backs, Gardnerand Parkinson ; forwards, Dawson, Downie, Lofthouse, Ralph, Turner, Redmond, Carney, Miller, and Jackson.—The St. Helens captain won the toss, and gave the home team the privilege of playing down the incline. The hone team pressed at the start, and Gardner:rushed over, and scored for the. home team amid loud cheers, which were repeated a moment later when Lambert steered the ball over the bar, thus scoring the major point.. From now to the call of half-time the game was of a very even description, the score at this period being Lancaster one goal, two minors ; Sc. Helens, nil. The change of ends saw St. Helens playing down the slope, and the Saints' for- wards, who were playing a good combined game, went with a rush with the ball at their feet, taking play close to the Lancaster goal line, where, from a splendid pass, Cross got possession and dropped a, splendid goal, thus making the score equal. After this desperate attempts were made by each side tv increase their score. From another scrimmage close to the Laneaster goal line. Foreman got possession and dashed ovtr, scoring a good try, but the kick at goal was a failure. The Saints afterwards had the best of the game, which ended in a victory for St. Helens by tone goal, one try, to one goal ' and two minors. RUNCORN V. MANCHBSTER nuns WAND/MM.—This match was played at Runcorn before a moderate atten- dance of spectators. The visitors arrived one man short, and a substitute was found in Hailwood. who did good work for them. Anderton, the Wanderer's captain, was also absent, being engaged doing battle with the Lan- cashire county team against the Maoris. Runcorn had also to call up reserves, both Faulkner and W. Hughes being absent, the latter being on the sick list; but we are glad to learn that he will be ready to help his club against the Old Boys to-day (Saturday), when we may expect to see a fine game of football, this fixture being considered one of the most attractive and also one of the best on the Runcorn card. Schofield kicked off for the Wanderers, and Brazendale returned. Hindle secured possession and punted well, and the Wanderers' for- wards dribbling on Rigby stepped into the breach and arrested the onward movement. After several short scrimmages, Gayter picked up and dashed across the line, thus scoring the first try. Woods kicking a goal. From a punt by Goldthorpe W. Riley obtained a free kick, which being well followed up a minor was regis- tered for Runcorn. Following the drop-out, Brazendale alfnost dropped a goal. Hindle, for the Wanderers, made a capital run, and punted to mid-field, where good passing was witnessed between Hughes and Evans. The Wanderers maintained their position for a little while. until Broady and Hancock dribbled to the visitors' quarter. Goldthorpe, Goward, and Dean then passed to each other with advantage, which, however, was neutra- lized by Woods taking a drop at goal, but the ball fell short. Wainwright a little later on also tried a similar shot without result. Broady restarted the game after half time, and Hughes exchanged kicks with Hindle, the latter punting to centre. Loose scrimmaging was now engaged in, and then Wainwright obtained the ball at the centre of the ground, and after a brilliant run gained a try. Following this success H. Hughes dodged his opponents splendidly, and got over the line. The pressure was still kept up when Stubbs ran in. The Wanderers now roused themselves up, and play was carried to neutral ground, W. Riley returning with a good punt. Broady passed to Wainwright, who ran well and then gave the ball to W. Riley, who caused play to lodge in the visitors' 25. Dean kicked to Brazendale, who ran very strongly, and after being collared put in a good punt. Just before time H. Hughes ...again scored. Final result :—Runcorn three goals, two tries, five minors. Manchester Wanderers nil Runcorn: Brazendale, full back; three-quarters, G. T. Wainwright, T. Woods, W. A. Riley; half, H. Hughes (captain) and W. Evans; forwards, W. 11. Broady, F. Hancock, R. Dolan, J. Gayter, W. Stubs, W. Shaw, J. Rigby, J. Bowyer, and P. Riley. Free Wanderers: Full back, H. Holt; three-quarters, T. Hindlf, J. Anderton Goldthorpe, F. Kennedy; half, E. C. Holt and A. R. Dean; forwards, W. Schofield (captain), J. Worthing- ton, T. Taylor, E. McClure, W. H. Longworth, L. Goward, C. E. Walker, R. Hailwood. WARRINGIibN "A " T. TITHBOOK IST Teaac—Played on the Wilderspool gound on Saturday. Pearson kicked off for the visitors, Bate returning to centre. From the scrimmage the visitors carried play to the home 25, and Bailey getting hold, he put in a good kick, the ball going dead. Mather dropped out, and Pearson returned to centre. A grand dribble, headed by Donoghue, Rat- cliffe, and Bate, carried play to the visitors' 25. From a scrimmage Berry passed to Speakman, who transferred to Appleton' this player kicking our the line, a minor resulting. Soon afterwards Jolley obtained 'possession, and kicked to the Tuebrook 25, and the Warrington forwards, headed by Beard, Adamson, Ratcliffe, and Isherwood, following up well, prevented a return. A scrimmage was formed opposite the visitors' goal posts, When a good rush by the home team forced a minor. Tuebrook dropped out, and play rested in their 25. From the ensuiqg scrimmage Butcher kicked to Jolley, who made his mark. No advantage being gained, play raged in neutral territory, where Appleton stopped a dangerous rush by the visitors by kicking into touch. Warburton got a pass, and made a good drop at goal. Pearson saving by touching down. Warburton replied to the drop-out by kicking to Pearson, who kicked into touch. From a pack Astbury passed to Morriss, who made a nice run, but was checked by Appleton. Adamson, Hayes, Molyneaux, and Creaghan carried play to the visitors' 25, Pearson saving nicely. From a line-out Mather passed to Warburton, who got away and took another drop at goal, the ball going dead. Bailey was next conspicuous by a goodirun up the field, but was tackled by Jolley. The visitors, headed by Western, Holloway, and Butcher, carried play over the home line, enabling the last-named player to score a try, which was not improved. Jolley dropped out, Pearson returning to centre. Mather put in a good kick, and good following up by Donoghue, Bate, Creaglaan, and Beard prevented a return. Soon afterwards the home forwards took play back to the visitors' territory,where they were allowed a free kick for off-side tackling. Warburton took the place , kick, the ball just missing the goal posts, a minor ensu-

ing. Half-time was now called, the score being— Warrington, 5 minors; Tuebrook, 1 try and 1 minor. Isherwood restarted, and play rested in Tuebrook 29. From the scrimmage the visitors rushed the oval up the field to Warrington territory. Warburton relieved by a good kicirto centre. Tuobrook paid another flying visit to Warrington quarters, the ball going into touch. From the line-out Butcher passed to Bailey, who failing to gat hold, enabled Appleton to kink to neutral ground. Tuebrook brought play back in Warrington 25, where, from a scrimmage, Hayes, Beard, Molyneaux, and Ratcliffe, were conspicuous by a good dribble to the visitors' line. Tuebrook seen afterwards relieved te ceetre. The Warrington forwards worked the oval back to the visitors' territory, where they pressed for some time, until Tuebrook relievedby a desperate effort, carrying play to centre. Jolley obtained possession and put in a good-kick to the visitors' 25; and quick follow- ing up by Beard, Appleton, and Speakman enabled Appleton to get over the line, but the ball was ruled back. A scrimmage was formed near to the line, from which Appleton received a pass and dashed over, the try being again disallowed, and a minor resulting. The drop-out brought no relief. The Tuebrook forwards carried play to centre, where Jolley returned to Pearson', who replied to centre, and Bailey headed a dribble, taking the oval over the home line, a minor ensuing. Jolley droppeflout,Bailey returning inte touch. Warrington were allowed a free kick for a knock on, and no retwn being made play rested in the centre, where from a scrimmage the home forwards, headed by Beard, Adamson, and Donoghue, carried play to the Tuebrook 25. From the scrimmage Mather got posaessien and dashed over the line, scoring a good try, Warburton making a rod attentpt for goal. Shortly after the whistle blew her He side," the game ending in a draw, the score being as follows:—Warrington, 1 try and 8 misers; Tuebrook, 1 try and 2 minors. Teams :—Warrington A: T. Jolley, full back ; A. Appleton, J. Speakman, and W. Warbur- ton, three-quarter backs; S. Mather and J. Berry, half backs; Adamson (captain), Creaghan, Ishervroed, Donoghue, Molyneaux, Beard, Hayes. ltstcliffe, and Bate, forwards. Tuebrook: H. Pearson, full back; J. Bailey, T. Bailey, and E.?. Morriss, three-quarter backs; J. Astbury, and J. Butcher, half backs; VI, T. Holloway (captain), S. J. Holloway, T. Western, J. Grundy, L. Vickers, J. J. Lines, T. Fletelier, A. J. Pearson, and W. L. Goodman, forwards. WARRINGTON v. BARROW.

One of the many pleasant ntatchee on the Warrington card, and one ever awaited with the greatest pleasure by the" vrirepullers," took place on Saturday, whoa the Warrington beam journeyed to Barrow, to try conclusions with the premier club of that town. Splen- did weather favoured the match, although the turf was of a slippery nature. Only a moderate attendance wit- netsed the encounter, this fact, being due, no doubt, to the lock-out which at present unfortunately prevails in the district. Arriving in good time an early start was decided on, and when the team faced each other, Jolley and Dillon were found to be absentees en the Warrington side, the latter's service being required by the Lancashire County in their match with the Maoris. At 2.45 Harley started operations with a huge kick. Off side play ruled a pack at neutral ground,and Evans being wrongly tacklal, the same player was allowed a free kick. This was eagerly followed up by the visiting team, and Woodburn being pressed, he mulled the oval, and allowed Handles, Littlewood, and Ashurst to take the leather over, the last-named securing a try in the first minute. Barnes, however, failed at place. This success of the Warringtonians apparently roused the home team, but despite the cheers of their supporters they could not pre- vent the "wirepuliers" from adopting an aggres- sive attitude. Momentary relief was brought about by Harley, but Speakman by a strong kick placed the hoe:testers at their original position. Give,and-take play followed, until Speakman enlivened the monotony by a tricky run, and dodging his opponents with accur- acy, the visitors had the satisfaction of adding try num- trar2. Again Barnes failed at goal. From the drop-out Barnes; and Massey executed some smart work, until Forshaw came to the rescue of his side by a sterling run to neutral ground. Exertions by the Barrow forwards were easily frustrated, and Povey elicited cheers for a smart dribble. Harley endeavoured to force an opening, and partly succeeded, until Massey brought him to grass at half way flag. Quick passing by the Barrow backs ended in Gregory getting in, but a pass forward ruled the oval back at the quarter flag, from which place Barnes and Massey by judicious kicks placed the game at the Barrow quarters. Barrios now had a narrow shave for goal, the oval just going on the outside. After Harley had executed some neat work, Antrobus dogded round the pack, taking t,he leather over, Bandies completing the try, and Frank Turner failing at the place. Barnes responded to the drop-out, and a free kick t Daniels again harassed the home defence, and although a chance was missed, Harley eventually had an abet-- the shot at goal, which brought about half time, Warrington having three tries two minors to their credit against a minor. With the substantial lead of three tries, Frank Turner started,and only a faint reply was made. The Barrow men now played with renewed vigour, and for a time the Warrington citadel was in jeop- ardy. Harley had another ineffectual shot at goal, and directly after Gregory experienced hard lines in not scor- ing, for he got over, but failed to ground, Evans knocking him into touch-in-goal. The visitors allowed the Furness men a short stay in their quarters, and then a combined rush, in which Frank Turner, Ashton, and Unswerth ' played a prominent part, transferred operations to the Barrow 25. Frank Turner now got clear away, but when scoring seemed a certainty, he passed unself- fishly to his comrades and Harley, being in attendance, intercepted and placed the game at neutral ground. Handles was next to the fore with a smart try, but through some informality the point was disallowed. Grand passing by Antrobus, Speakman, and Barnes was watched with interest, the ball ultimately gravitating in touch at the Barrow quarter-flag. Harley got the oval away, but Barnes was equal to Aire occasion, and responded gallantly. A rush, headed by: Littlewood, almost notched a tangible point, and again the visiting backs treated the onlookers to a grand display of passing. Daniels was hold close to the line, and later on, Povey showed up with a neat dribble, which certainly deserved a better fate. Harley affarded relief for his side, and neutral ground was once more the scene of operations. From now to the call of time the visitors contented themselves with keeping thoir orponents at bay, and the last point of interest was a strong run by Aatrobus, who dashed away to the Barrow line, when time was called with the score—Warrington, 0-3-2; Barrow, 0-0-2.

• Undoubtedly Warrington owe their success to their better combination and superior forward play. The front van always had the measure of their opponents, and whenever preesure was brought to bear, it only required a slight effort on the forwards' part to place the game at the Barrow quarters. Their play was characterized by three strong points, viz., dribbling, accurate tackling, and smart following up. The backs, too, were far superior to the Barrow representatives, and altheugh the score was only three trice, no extra exertion warmade when the Warringtonians had gained their substantial lead.

_ The teams were as follows :—Warrington J. W. Evans, back; Daniels, T. Barnes, and J. T. Massey, three- quarter backs; W. Speakman and A. Antrobus, half backs; H. Ashton, Fair Turner, W. Povey, R. Little- wood, W. Nevins, Frank Turner, C. Unsworth, W. Bandies, and A. Askurst, forwards. Barrow: Wood- burn back ; Gregory, Harley, and Porshkw, three- quarter backs ; Whitehead ' and Chubb, half basis; Kinnish, Abbott. Troughton, Todd, Mutch, Alexander, Ferguson, Smith, and Haynes, forwards. After the match the Warrington team were hospitably entertained by the Barrow club.

"SOUTH AFRICA ; ITS PEOPLES AND CUSTOMS." An interesting lecture, on " South Africa ; its Peoples and Customs." was given in the Baptist Chapel, Latchford, on Thursday evening last week by the Rev. J. W. Varley. Councillor H. Roberta presided, and there was a large attendance: Having made a passing allusion to his own residence in South Africa, Mr. Varley remarked upon the diver- sity and races that were to be met with there, such as Malays, Hottentots, Kaffirs--which was rather a general name—Grikua, gaika, Terabit, Tambookies, Basuto, Zulu, Bushmen, Pingo, and also the Dutch boor. The Malays he described as usefal as fishers, water-carriers, and porters, and par- ticularly skilful as workers in wood. The Dutch boere— boar being the Dutch name for farmer—ivere, he said, great haters of the English people, and this hatred the lecturer attributed largely to the abolition of slavery in 1834, when the Boers were compelled to "trek" away into the Orange Free State and ultimately into the Transvaal. In appearance the boars are strongly-built, with narrow, fore- heads, bushy eyebrows, and high, cheekbones. and heads surmounted by an immense hat. Their mental status was not very high, though educa- tion was now more sought after than formerly. As.an instance of the boers' ignorance of other countries Mr. Tarley mentioned that they believed the thousand troops or thereabouts that . were engaged in the first engagement in the Transvaal comprised the whole of the British army. A boer's farm was usually from 2,000 to 10,000 acres in extent. He was very indolent, and only grew enough corn to seive. for his own household. His live stock consisted mainly of sheep and ostriches and these wore looked after by a few Hottentots. Lithe morning the farmer would get up at sunrise and would let the sheep out of the kraal counting "them as they came out. They were then given into the charge of the Hottentots who took them away to where there was grass and water, and who • r )nght them back at sun- down when they wore again counted. This custom the. lecturer pointed out wee an interesting illustration of the parable of the shepherd. The boors were very hospitable, especially if you could smoke and take what they called a " sopie '—that was to say if you could drink whiskey. (Laughter.) Owing to the scarceness of bricks the beer's house was generally built of compressed mud, and the walls, as A rule, were from two to three feet thick. The fire-place was not in the Old Tudor style, and the rooms very often have the appearance of a newly-swept chimney. Along by the rafters there was very fre- quently a shelf which acted as a receptacle for rats and mice, tortoise and spiders, and sometimes for a snake. There was any number of pots and dishes lying about and the general appearance was very much like what you might suppose the world to have presented when it was void and without form. (Laughter.) Having referred to the Bushmen and Hottentots, Mr. Varley next dealt with the Kaffirs. Captain Barrow says that these people are descended from the Arabs, and that, three or four centuries ago they came down the south-east coast of Africa. In figure they are muscular and symmetrical, elegant in deportment; frank, fearless, generous and very intelligent. The young are wild, petulant, and unreasoning, but the old are shrewd, sagacious,and have great political wisdom. In the towns they are employed in various capacities. They seem to have two principal reasons for working in the town—one was that they might buy a gun, and the other that they might save sufficient money to buy cattle to exchange for a wife. Polygamy is very prevalent amongst them and the wife Is always bought with from two to one hundred head of cattle, according to her social condition. The wife is really a slave, and has to plough and to •sow and gather in the corn at harvest time. Instances were next given lof Kaffir superstition and cruelty. Speaking with regard to the future of Africa; the lecturer saikthat the verdict of history was that centuries ago the people et that continent had been' 'foremost in the arts, and in COM- merceand civilisation.. The main cause of their present depression was,the slaVe -trade. What was wantel was a firm hand telbreak up the Arabs who were decimating and-desolatiag the vast fertile regions of central Africa, and Christianity would do a great deal towards elevating and ennobling the heart and lives of the black tribes of Africa. (Hear hear, and applause.) He contended that races which bad produced . such men as ithanasius, Origen, St. Augustan, Arnobius, and Cyprien, and had' risen to such a height of civilisation as was seen in ancient Carthage, were not beyond redemption. (Loud applause.)—The Chairman commented in eulogistic terms on the merits of the lecture, and expressed a hope that Mr. Varley would give a series.—Councillor W. Pierpoint moved, Dr. Goruall seconded, and Mr. W. Davidson supported, a vote of thanks te the lecturer, which was cordially agreed o, and briefly responded to by Mr. Varley.

div.head: NOTES,, BY . THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES,, BY . THE WAY.

Warrington found some solace for their defeat by Wakefield Trinity on the previous week in the conclusive drubbing they were enabled to inflict upon Barrow on Saturday afternoon. The game was fought on the Barrow ground but the home team were scarcely ever in it from beginning ,to end, the final score standing at three tries and two minors to two minors.

The hitherto invincible " A " team of Warrington found a hard nut to crack in Tuebrook, and in fact did not succeed in quite cracking it, though they managed to keep their record inviolated by defeat. The game, which took place on the Warrington ground, was a draw in favour of the home players by one try and six minors to one try and two minors. It was a near shave, however, for Tnebrook, who played a really fine game, were lead- ing by a try up to within a few minutes of the end. This was largely due to the fact that Warrington did not play their usual combination, the team being con- siderably weakened in some of its parts. W. Dillon, of Warrington, was again in the County team in the match with the Maoris at Whalley Range, on Saturday. The New Zealanders made a stout fight against Lancashire's representatives and the latter were only able to secure a verdict by one try and three minors to two minors, Out of the 27 matches which the Maories had played in this country up to Saturday night they had won 17, lost eight, and drawn two, a 'pretty good record considering that they have mostly met first- class teams. On Wednesday the New Zealanders scored a notable victory over Yorkshire County by two goals, four tries, and one minor, to one nal, three tries, and nvo minors. The Yorkshire team was not the same that defeated Lancashire.

We understand that the toui of the Warrington team has now been definitely arranged. On Saturday, Feb. 16th, they will meet Leeds Parish Church at Leeds, Marylebone on the following Monday, Rugby on Tues- day, and Burton on Wednesday. The annual meeting of county representatives to arrange the fixtures of the cricket season was held on Tuesday at Lord's. A number of county matches were arranged, Northumberland and Lincolnshire swelling the already long list of counties with regular elevens. All the usual fixtures—such as Oxford and Cambridge, Eton and Harrow, Gentlemen and Players—are retained; and there will, contrary to the precedentsof recent years, be no fewer than four North and South matches—one at the Oval, one at Lord's, a third at Manchester, and a fourth at the end of the Scarborough Cricket Festival in September. There is to be no week at Cheltenham, and Lancashire will not meet Derbyshire.

div.head: YILIERAL OF THE LATE DR. SMITH.
div.p: YILIERAL OF THE LATE DR. SMITH.

The funeral of the late Dr. Joseph Smith took place on Saturday afternoon, when the mortal remains of the deceased ' gentleman were conyeyed to their last resting place at the Warrington ceme- tery. The funeral procession left the late residence of the deceased, 27 Wilson-Patten-street, at two o'clock, and proceeded to Bold-street Chapel, where a abort and solemn service was held. Thence the procession started for the cemetery in the following order .—First, members- of the congregation : second, carriage containing the ministers of the circuit ; and third, the hearse. Then followed nine carriages, con- taining Dr. T. Starkey Smith, Mr. Joseph Smith (sons of fhe deceased) • Mr. Kidd, Mr. John Starkey, Mr. Reginald Smith, Mr. Stanley Kidd, Mrs. Robert Garnett, Mrs. Coop; Councillors Hutchinson, Wm. Pierpoint, J. 13. Wright, Shaw-Green; and John Pierpoint • Dr. Gornall, and several other gentlemen. The service at the grave side was read by rhe Rev. G. E. Young, and amongst those there present were Drs. White, Goma% Fox, Cannel!, and Jack: Mr. William Sharp, and the Rev. 8, Wilkinson. The funeral arrangements had been entrusted to:Messrs. Robert Garnett and Sons, by whom the coffin' which was covered with wreaths, was sup- plied. It was of fumed oak, with pannelled lid and brass mountings. and on the plate were the words "Joseph Smith, born January 15th, 1812 ,died Decem- ber sth, 1888." The carriers were Messrs. William Tinsley, John Marsh, Edwin Longshaw, and Thomas Daly, the last-named having been in the service of the deceased for a considerable number of years. Amongst those present at the funeral service in Bold-st. PCkapel werii the Rev. G. E. Young (superintendent of the circuit), the Revs. W. Brookes, and B. H. Jackson; the Mayor (Alderman Sutton); Aldermen Burgess, Har- rison, and Holmes; Councillor R. W. Marsh; Dr. T. Starkey Smith, and several relatives of the deceased; circuit stewards, Mr. Wm. Silcock and Mr. R. G. Hen- shall; society stewards, Mr. J. J. Sanderson, and Mr. W. Nicholson; poor stewards, Mr. John Toft, and Mr. John Taylor; chapel stewards, Mr. T. B. Garter and Mr. Prince; Dr. White; Messrs. Robert Garnett, Wm. Barlow F. Dixon, J. Hall, John Bennett, E. Richardson, W. Collier, S. B. Stringer, W. J. Horton, S. Hunt (chief constable), Wm. Gleave, J. T. Pattison, E. Dallow, John Hartley, Jabez Pliaston, and Wm. Roberts. The pulpit was draped in black. The first part of the burial service was read by the Rev. G. E. Young, and the second part by the Rev. E. H. Jackson. Then an appropriate hymn was sung, and prayer offered by the Rev. W. Breokes, after which, The Rev. G. E. Young addressed the congregation. Few men, he supposed, were at one time better known in the town and neighbourhood than the late Dr. Joseph Smith. He was prominent both in the church with which he was connected and generally in public lift. His life, he believed, was begun in Manchester, and he became when yet a young man thoroughly decided for Christ. From what he had heard, and from his intercourse with him during the last two years, he had every reason to believe that the late Dr. Smith, was, as many of them understood, truly converted to God. He was remarkably earnest and energetic in every kind of werk he undertook, whether it was work in the church or outside, and many of their friends, he had no doubt, remembered that he was a most acceptable and 'useful local preacher. He occupied pulpits in Methodism both in this ,iind in other towns, and very frequently in ithe country part of the circuit, and many times hail he heard friends in the country talk of the services which had been conducted by Dr. Smith. lie was very well- known at Bold-street as a class leader; and it was only a few days ago that he heard one of their older friend, say that he remembered the time when the late Dr. Smith used to have no fewer than 30 or 40 persons present at his week-night class meeting. Dr. Smith had a very extensive practice ma surgeon, but notwith- standing all the claims it had upon him he found time to render wonderful service to the church. He was pro- minent not only in the spiritual but in the temporal affairs of the church, and occupied the highest positional Methodism could confer upon a layman, while he was always ready to engage in good works. He understood' the deceased had a great deal to do 'with the scheme for, the erection of Bewsey-road Chapel, and he was always ready to help with his purse; and whilst thoroughly attached to the church of his choice he was by no means a narrow, bigoted sectarian, but a true catholic. Dr. Smith was once Mayor of the borough, and for many years a justice of :he peace, and ho had heard someof their public men say how very honourably and efficiently he discharged the duties appertaining to those important offices. About ten years ago he was smitten dowliby a terrible affliction, and during the last two months ho had been in great weakness and had suffered much, but he (Mr. Young) could tell the congregation that he never came away from a visit to him without feeling, a betteriman.

div.head: MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
div.p: MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.

The first concert for the present season of the Warrington Musical Society was given in the Public Hall, on Tuesday evening, before a large and fashionable audience. The., Society has recently had a considerable addition to its members, and the small adverse balance with which last season closed has been cleared off. Handel's "Alexander's Feast " constituted the first part of the programme. It is not one of the great composer's most import- ant or best known works, although there is one magnificient air—" Revenge, Timotheus cries I"— which is often sung at high-class concerts. The principal artistes were Misses Ada Lee and Rose M. Gurton (sopranos), Miss Unsworth (contralto), Mr. Thomas Barlow (tenor), and Mr. Arnold J. Cleaver (baritone). Miss Lee possesses a voice which is of fine quality, and particularly sweet, although its range is not the most extensive. She knows, too, how to manage her voice to a nicety, and therefore sung with excellent effect: She was especially successful in the passage beginning "The Prince unable to conceal his pain." and in " Timotheus placed on high." Mr. Barlow also acquitted him- self very creditably, and showed himself fully equal to the large share of vocalism which fell to him as tenor in "Alexander's Feast." Mr. Cleaver had less to do, but he did that little well, and he was heartily applauded for his rendering of the air "Revenge, Tiniotheus cries." Of the chorus more cannot be said than that they did fairly well. There was an uncertainty of attack in various passages which suggested the deed of more rehearsing. No doubt the fact that the members of the Society have had in hand the 'production of the " Messiah,' 'as well as this concert, will have something to do with this want of preparedness. It is satisfactory to note that there is a large number of good vocalists of every class, (150 altogether) and that. there is, therefore, plenty of material, with sufficient training for the most successful m.usical perfermances. 'The second part of the concerf opened with Gounod's chorus "0 sing unto the Lord.' Miss Unsworth distinguished her- self in this composition by singing the solo allotted to her very tastefully and very powerfully, and it is a mattfr of course to say that she was heartily applauded. Loneellow's poem of The Singers," with music by Mr. F. If. Kinsey, was admirably sung by Mr. Cleaver. The chorus took up the last verse, and sang it with capital effect. The com- poser, Mr. Kinsey. himself accompanied, and it is scarcely necessary to say that he made the best of a tuneful and expressive composition. - He was recalled, along with Mr. Cleaver, and the last three verses were resung. Mr. G. T. Drif- field, the organist, next executed an organ solo, slow movement from Sonato, "The maid of Orleans" (Sterndale Bennett.) This perform- ance was an exceedingly skilful one, and was highly appreciated. The Society is fortunate in having an organist of Mr. Driffield's qualifications. The organ itself is not in the best of repute, but it is due to the organist to say that for once he brought more delightful sound out of it than it was thought there Was in it. If time had per- mitted, the audience were in the mood for insisting upon an encore. Miss Ada Leo sang with sweetness and finish the recitative and aria " Ernani Invo- lami " (Verdi), which is well suited to her voice. Mr. Barlow then rendered "Only once more," a sopg whieh is very musical as to its refrain„ but is so inconsequential as to meaning that rothing much can be made of it. The.concert closed with a red- dering of "The Feast of Adonis," by Jensen. The chorus made a very good start with this com- position, and throughout sustained the excellent impression which they made, the buoyant and tuneful passages being satisfactorily presented. The solos were sung by Miss Gunton, but not in a manner which calls or any special comment. Dr. Hiles, as usual, ably conducted, and Mr. W. S. Woods efniently accompanied. The concert commenced at 7.30, and was brought to a close,by. 9.45. It was something of a drawback to those wilip were making use of a special train to Latchford and Lymm, and they had to wait until 10.30.

Tue " Messiah " will be performed by the Society on Monday evening next, the special vocalists engaged being Mademoiselle Antoinette Trebelli, Miss Eleanor Rees Mr. Henry Piercy, and Mr. Bridson. There will be a full band, and as the chorus and instrumentalists will be familiar with the music, there is every reason to anticipate an admirable performance.

div.p: Zetter to the itor.

THE QUESTION OF BAPTISM. Sir,—Whilst Mr. Foulke's in his excellent letter points out the errors regarding baptism, as taught at Frodsham' he does not say a word on believer's baptism as taught us by precept and example by our blessed Saviour. There are many texts to prove it is according to the Scriptures as much as the Lord's Supper. That ordin- ance, as a body of believers, we acknowledge. I have thought much on this subject and have wondered how it is every Christian cannot see it their duty to follow our Saviour's loving command, Mark 16th chap. 16th verse, 28th Matthew 19th 20th verses., Acts 2nd 38th 41st verses. Believer's baptism is as plain as the sun when it shines in its meridian splendour. Let us dedicate our children to God in their infancy, and train them for Him to the utmost, and leave baptism in its right place.—l remain, sir, faithfully yours, A LOVER OF TRUTH.

div.head: SMOKE AND LONDON FOGS.
div.p: SMOKE AND LONDON FOGS.

-... Sir,—! fully appreciate your remarks in your last impression re my lecture on Smoke and London Foes." When that paper was read it was given as an argumen- tative one, owing to so much being said concerning smoke being so much waste ; the cause of fogs—damage to buildings, choking people, killing plants and shrubs &c. What I desire to say now is this: My dust theory was ridiculed by the scientific and the unscien- tific, and now that it is proved and demonstrated by Mr. John Aitken, F.R.S.E., it is only right those people should know of it and reconsider their opinions. Questions such as : How is it London fogs are so thick ? How is it one can smell them, and that they have .an acid taste? were outside my argument that evening. That the fogs are thicker than they are in Faris I never did deny; but I contend that the immense vehicular and pedestrian traffic has to do with it, whilst the "blacks " emanating from the domestic fires assist in making them darker. The sulphurous vapours that are given off also hang in the air at inhaling height in such atmospheres, causing an offence to the nostrils and a choking sensation to the breathing organs. THOMAS MORRIS. Warrington, December 12, 1888.
MORE LIGHT AT EARLESTOWN.

Sir,—Will you allow me, through the medium of your valuable paper, to call the attention of the powers that be to what is, and has been for some years, a crying necessity. Those who are in the habit of going up the New Road to Crow-lane and Newton Common, will have noticed that after they leave the Baptist Chapel there is not another lamp till they get to Crow Lane. Now on a dark foggy winter's night many females do not dare to go, but wait until they either get some company or get a friendly ride in some conveyance. I presume the Commissioners, are waiting until all the land is built upon before they will put lamps down. It is very probable that will not be for many years to -come. There is also another place -where the necessity for more light is equally urgent; I refer to the Brow from Mr. Emmett's house to Mrs Heyes's at the Common Lock. It was reported the last time there was a man drowned that the Coroner very strongly urged the powers con- cerned to put some lamps down in that locality, at once. If that was so it is evident no notice has been taken of ic. Now as a ratepayer myself, I don't think the rate- payers generally would grudge to pay for a few addi- tional laanps that would be needed. Hoping the Commissioners will see their way to do this much-needed piece of work. I enclose my name, and remain, yours truly,
MORE LIGHT.

div.head: FREE LIBRARY SCHEME.
div.p: THE FREE LIBRARY SCHEME.

Sir,—l should like to know, what has become of the Free Library scheme. Is it dead or only refreshing itself with "forty winks." At any rate, I hope that its promoters have not dropped their work contented with the "penny per book dodge." If they are of the opinion that that system meets the requirements of the people on behalf of whom they agitated, they are under a delusion. I hope, Mr. Editor, that you will join with the workingmen who are so badly in need of help and favour the somnolent ones with an "eye-opener" With regard to the idea that the penny-per-book system is a step towards a Free Library, I should like to point out that a studious person, even if he—or she—be employed during the day, is easily able to digest the contents of 18 books in three months, or of 80 books per year. Supposing a man adopts the " Penny " system in place of the old is. ed. per quarter or ss. per year subscription, if he employs the most of his spare time in study, he will find the new system much more expensive than the eld. I have tried both systems and am now glad to go back to the quarterly subscription. This is the borrower's side of the question but I think it has been demonstrated pretty clearly, in theory here, and practically at St. Helens, that the increase in the rates caused by the maintenance of the library, is more than counter-balanced by the benefit to the country. I hope this matter will pet ke allowed quietly to slide into oblivion and that the miedis of the res'iee_" senate at the Town ifall Will be eccasionally " jogged" ITO eXamination of its dpoirOility,—Yeurs. ko
A PLEB.

Again, last Saturday's letter says, Ist "That Mr. Thornton must know that it is as reasonable to say the population of Warrington was unalterably fixed some years ago as to assert that the ground rent of the land on which Warrington stands was so fixed." Ground rent he says, "is the rent which is, or can be obtained for allowing the use of asite of land, and as surely as the population and trade of a town grow this rent will grow with them." My statement was that land leased for 999 years was unalterably fixed by law for that term, and that no alteration in taxes or assessments, or improvement in sites, nor value of property, could affect any change whatever. Suppose for a moment they could, what would be the property owners' and tenants' position? Why, simply open to be fleeced on both sides; on the one hand by the landowner, and on the other by the tax gatherer, for if based upon borough assessment, the shop I cited would not only be charged three times the amount of ra.e, but the landowner would treble his ground rent. I think that this will be patent to all readers. .

Second point to which " Economist " has shifted. That, in support of his contention, he says that "in very many cases rates are really paid out of an additional value which has been conferred on building sites, not by the owners of the buildings themselves, but by the inhabitants of the town as a whole." What does this mean? Why not only that" Economist" acknow- ledges himself in a fog, but clearly, and at one sweep, throws all his other arguments to the ground, for the inhabitants pay the rates, whether in part or a whole, how can t'.e landowner pay them? Surely the col- lectors don't ask for rates twice. But I emphatically deny, and did so in my last, that landowners pay borough rates at all. The only taxes they pay are to Government, and I again repeat that borough rates, come from the property owners and occupiers only and it is a shame they should; it is a matter that requires looking into. "Economist" says "that if rates were abolished t would neither affect property owners, nor occupiers, but simply the landowners." This it so clearly wrong that I leave it with the reader. " Economist " then finishes his letter by saying that" Mr. Thornton is fond of statistics" and gives me a case "to harmonize with my theory" as follows: —" Within the last few months the rents of certain cottages in Warrington have been raised by 6d. and 3d. a week, the reason as given by the owner being, not that the rates have been raised, but that owing to to the influx of workers on the Ship Canal, the demand for such cottages had grown." If "'Economist " had been the owners of the said cottages, no doubt he could have answered this himself, especially if he had bough' and paid the price at which property was sold at, before the panic, for it is well known that property has gone down during the panic about 25 per cent. Property owners have suffered severely, from raised assessment, empty houses, and reduced rents; I know myself of some cases, where the rents collected have very little more, if any, than cleared the rates and repairs. In fact in some cases there has been heavyloss. Shops ,too,have gone down in proportion. So that it may be that the cottages " Ecconomist " names were lowered in rents, and the present 3d. and 6d. rise, may not even cover the loss, by bringing the cottages up to their original rents.—Yours truly,
H. THORNTON. The Laurels Fearnhead Cross, Dec. 12, 1883.
