div.p: Warrington, Dec. 11th, 1888.

"WHO PAYS RATES." • Sir,—Don't you think that it is a great mistake for a man like 'E nomist " with such brilliancy of thought, extensive knowledge, and unparalleled writing ability, to be so very soon drawn out to display his temper, and show his teeth? He is simply exposing his own disposi- tion and exhibiting the weakness of his arguments. Several ratepayers have named the matter to me, and said how foolish and weak-minded he must be, and that he ought to be glad to be put straight so soon, on such an important matter, before he indiscreetly happens to repeat his already manifested ignorance, before company who might mercilessly expose his folly. Since you are theonly person supposed to know whom Si Economist" is, I feel sure that he would reap great personal advantages, if either yourself, or some other sufficiently intelligent individual, could be found to approach him, and out of charity volunteer a few whole- some words of advice. Out of sympathy, I will do my best to make him understand if he will call at my office, some day when I have nothing of importance in hand. The best plan, however, would- be for him to accept my last suggestion—"buy some property," or pay a heavy rent. Of course lam supposing that "Economist" may only be a lodger; and still it seems wanting, to imagine even, that he is not a wealthy man, seeing that he is an "Economist" and so exceptionally accomplished. For many reasons, it is a pity thathis real name does not appear. :This being so, however, we must do the best we can under thecircumstances, by correspondence. Let us again examine "Economist's' own statements. He says that it is strange that I should fall into the mis- take of supposing that his first article was a reply to a statement made by me. That is surely an attempted subterfuge to shirk the question, since bah the attack and object, were too transparent. Let me inform him that it won't do ; the working classes and ratepayers of Warrington arc not to be gulled in that way. He implies that I made a foolish and illogical statement, when I said that the rates of the borough come from the property owners and tenants. Let him prove it; his last letter only weakens his first and confirms my statement. He says that I pretend to quote a great deal from his article, but scarcely once do I quote correctly, or fairly. He had better read the article referred to again, and considering that he is so effervescent and impetuous, it will be well if he will ask the aid of some well-wishing friend who is calmer and more collected. He accuses me ef saying "a deal about the wasteful manner iir which the rates of Warrington have been spent." This is simply untrue; I did not so much as name it. My points were, increased assessments, and rates, and that the rates are paid by property owners and occupiers, and not by the landowner as he asserts. But let me say, that the question of rate expenditure, amongst other matters affecting the government of this i borough, must and will be dealt with n due course, for there are burning questions, requiring determined and persisten. watching by the ratepayers. Never mind the gentlemen referred to by "Economist" whose opinions may or may not be more accurate than mine. • Economist says that he does not know whether or not the rates haVe been well or badly spent," and still in the same breath he says "that we have some tangible results to show," and he gives the following, "lessened death rate, Town Hall, the recreation grounds, a museum, and a library partially free, improved streets, and commodious market, and a hospital." Continuing, he says, "but whether these and other things are an exact equivalent for the rates that have been spent, is a complex problem which he does not attempt to solve." Let me ask could not " Economist " get a "scientific answer deduced from a consideration of economic principles or laws ?" These however are points which don't bear exactly upon the main question at issue, and which will be taken up in future criticism.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCILS. THE CHESHIRE ELECTION,
div.p: COUNTY COUNCILS. THE CHESHIRE ELECTION,

Baron von Schroeder, High Sheriff of Cheshire, has fixed Saturday, January 19, for the county elections in Cheshire and the first meeting of the new Council will be held on April 1, but the place of meeting has yet to be selected. Contests will take place in 24 divisions, in each case a Liberal being faced by a Tory, althougis both parties profess to fight independently of politics. WIDNES DIVISION.

At the weekly meeting of Widnes Local Board, on Tuesday, Mr. F. H. Gossage, presiding, the Clerk read the following letter, dated 29th November :—" I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknow- ledge the receipt of your letter of the 22nd instant, asking them to receive a deputation from the Widnes Local Board, to confer on the subject of the representa- tion of the district on the County Connell to be elected for Lancashire. The Board direct me to state that the formation of electoral divisions has been expressly entrusted by the Local Government Act to the Court of Quarter Sessions, and the Board could not undertake to interfere with their, decision prior to the first election, assuming that they arer empowered to. do so. Under these circum- stances the Board saw no advantage in the pro- posed interview. If the Local Board were dissatisfied with the number of County Councillors assigned to their district, they can after We County Council come into office, take steps with a view to getting the electoral divisions altered under section 54 of the Local Govern- ment Act." The Chairman said that letter showed that the local Board could not do anything further at pre- sent. He had been requested by the High Sheriff of Lancashire to assist him by becoming deputy returning officer for Whines Division, and he had consented to do so. (Hear, hear.) He had also agreed that the Town Hall and office staff should be used for the purposes of the election; of course the expenses would be paid by the central authority. The questions for the Board! now to consider were, who ought to be the candidate, and whether there would be a cont"sted election. From what he had heard he thought that two or three gentlemen would be nominated and that afterwards an arrangement might be entered into to avoid a competitive election. He was not in aposition to divulge names at present. If necessary he would call a public meeting to consider the question, and he sug- gested that in the meantime a special meeting should be held to consider the positiOn.—lt was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Brown seconded by Mr. W. W. Gossage to hold a special meeting on Tuesday afternoon next. During the present week a deputation of ratepayers waited upon Mr. Muspratt and formally solicited his permission to nominate him as a candidate, and it is generally understood that he consented, and amongst those usually well informed it is considered that Mr. Muspratt will be accepted without opposition as a most suitable representative of the town. RUNCORN.

The aspect of affairs in Runcorn has undergone an important change during the past week. On Tuesday evening a meeting of the Liberal Council was held in Itettlescl ketore Hall. 4bout half ,* doien names Were suggested, ana'a haUo vias ta with the Mott that Mr. Jas. Handley, J.P., and Mr. Wm. Ockldlston stere selected. Upon further consideration, it was tesolved to ask Mr. Handley to contest the South Division against Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., and Mr. Ockleston ,to do battle in the north division. A deputation was ' appointed to put the views of the Council before these gentlemen. We learn that Mr. Handley declines to accede to the invitation. Mr Ocklesten places his ser- vices at the disposal of the Council, and those who know him doubt not that he will . make a gallant fight against the odds that seem likely to be arrayed against him. FRODSHAM DIVISION.

. -----.. An enthusiastic meeting of Mr. Slater Lewis's sup- porters was held at Norley, in the Temperance Hall, on Mondayevening. Mr. John Gerrard occupied the chair. In introducing Mr. Lewis to the meeting, the Chairman said they had in him a gentleman who had had to battle with life, and who knew what it was to make his way in the world. They wanted representatives who knew how to earn money, and then they would know how to spend it. (Applause.)—Mr. J. Slater Lewis, who was cordially received, said he offered himself not as the representative of any class, but as the representa- tive of everybody—rich and poor alike. His opponent, Mr. Reynolds, was a most estimable man as a private gentleman—(hear, hear)—but did they want to make the new Act a dead letter by sendiAg county magistrates to represent them on the Council? ("No.") He had never seen Mr. Reynolds' name once as having been pre, sent at the Quarter Sessions, and although Mr. Reynolds 'was a member (ex-officio) of the Highway Board—he (Mr. Lewis)—having missed no meetings for four or five years, had never seen his face. Me would do Mr. Reynolds justice,—he had attended the Assessment Com- mittee most religiously, and was responsible, with others. for the ratepayers being landed in a lawyers bill of about £2,000 over the Ship Canal assessment appeal. His other opponent, Mr. Baxter, who offered him- self as a tenant farmers' candidate, was scarcely worthy of notice, as he had admitted through the press that he would retire, if required, in favour of Mr. Linaker. Mr. Lewis then spoke at great length on the County Council and was applauded on resuming his seat.—Mr. Wright moved and Mr. Hardman seconded a vote of confidence . . . . .

ist Mr. Lewis, which was carried. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close.—Mr. Lewis has already addressed about six meetings—all of which have been unanimous in his favour. A meeting of Mr. Lewis's supporters was held at Frodsham Bridge on Wednesday night, under the presidency of Mr. Shore, and after hearing an address from the candidate, a unanimous vote of confidence in him was passed.

Tian MCMIYEI OF A SISTER-IN-LAW.—At Belfast Assizes- , on Thursday, John Lennon, farmer, residing. near Dun- dalk, was found guilty of the murder of his sister-in-law, Annie M`Manus, on the 13th September last, while in a state of unsound mind, and was ordered by Justice Holmes to be detained in custody as a criminal lunatic during her Majesty's pleasure.

div.head: SHIP CANAL " GRABBBIt."
div.p: SHIP CANAL " GRABBBIt."

In " Cassell's Family Magazine" for December there is an interesting article on the Manchester Ship Canal which is adorned' with three striking illustrations. By the kind permission of the. pub- lishers, we are enabled to reproduce Um view which they give of the mechanical "Grabber" at work between Warrington and Runcorn. There are several "grabbers" at work on different sections of the Canal, and their method of working is watched with interest by many visitors to the works. A glance at the illustration will be sufficient to show that the machine is worked somewhat on the principle of a movable crane. The grabs, which in the illustration are open ready to descend, force their powerful, claws or teeth into the clayey soil, and, closing, bring away with them a considerable quantity of material, which is swung round in the same way as is the soil in the bucket of a steam navy, until it reaches a position over a train of waggons. The mechanism then causes the grabs to open again, and the material drops into a waggon. This Operation is repeated over and over again with sur- prising rapidity, and during a day's working a large amount of soil is dealt with. These machines can be used for a. variety of purposes, such as dredging d :cks, harbours, and rivers, and for gold dredging; excavating for new docks, canals, and railway cuttings; cutting trenches for pipe laying; lifting grain, coal, coke, land, blasted rock, &t; pile drivine • or as an ordinary portable engine. One man only being required to work the machine, it is admirably adapted for contractor's purposes. There are three different types ef the bucket or grab, to suit the various classes of material to be dealt with, and these tools are made with capacities of three hundredweight tar three tons. We understand that the contractor for the Ship Canal works has had no less than twenty-four of them at different times, which speaks well for their efficiency. We take the following extract from " Caseell's Magazine The idea of a navigable waterway to Manchester is not a new one; and schemes were brought forward scores of years ago, which railways caused the abandonment of; but for ten years the idea has taken increasing hold of the citizens of Cottonopolis ; and on the 27th of Innei 1882, Mr. Daniel Adamson broached the plan to an assemblage at his own house at Didsbury, at which eleven mayors of municipalities were present. A provi- sional committee (of which Mr. AdanTson was appointed the first chairman) was formed, plans were approved, and a Bill was presented for Parliamentary sanction, and the House of Commons sanctioned the measure, whilst the House of Lords decided that "it is not expedient to proceed with this Bill in the present session of Farliannent." The long and costly Parliamentary proceedings which succeeded .form an epoch in private Bill legislation which needs no reference now. In.the end the Act was obtained ; and then came the monetary difficulty. Failing to find a response amongst the -financiers, the promoters appealed to the people of Lancashire, and obtained subscribers sufficient to enable them to commence the great project • and now it is being pressed on with vigour. On the nth of November, 188 T, the first sod was cut at Eastham (where the canal joins the estuary of the river Mersey) by the chairman of the Company—Lord Egerton. The Ship Canal com- mences at Eastham, on the south bank of the Mersey estuary, and it follows the course of the bank for above a dozen miles, and thence in a course nearly direct for the city of Manchester. Its total length is a little over thirty-five miles, divided into sections, on nearly all of -which a commencement of the work has been made; and the locomotive, the "steam navvy," the steam excavator, steam cranes, portable engines, pumping engines, and other contractors' plant are at work. The work to be done is Immense; the cuttings alone involve the removal of 44,428,575 cubic yards of earthwork—a seventh part of which is rock. At Eastharn a number of " steam navvies" are at work, " scooping " out maerial from a solid " face " of earth as easily as a grocer draws out a taste of cheese. These huge land- dredging buckets, as they inightbe described, will attack the marl or clay to be removed ; and so rapid is their grape, so vast their hold of the "face," that in some instances one has been found to pull off and place in wagons for removal 1,000 tons of marl in a day's work. The steam navvy claims more than a ton of coals daily, and costs about £2,000. The operations are changing the appearance of marshy flats and pastoral land near the Mersey: villages of huts have sprung up, sheds for locomotives bulk out in the landscape, huge cuttings are being made, and Vast spa cee are being filled with the earth thence drawn; whilst a vigorous life spreads itself along he line the canal is to take, and overflows in its eager jollity into the towns near; so that abodes of chemicals, of salt, and of boatmen have added thereto the bustling life of the navvy. It is a wonderful work ; the con- tract price is to be £5,750,000 ; it is to be completed within four years from the date of commencement.; it removes canals of olden date, such as that from Run- corn to Latchford ;it alters the course of railways to some extent ; it carries roads above its own course, and places water-supples under it ; it fills the beds of rivers ^ •.....ter.`COUTfietS • nrrAll Tag 1005 44471 1111,11005. hydraulic tnacinneiy, Mail' swing is t steel- work in the girders for the bridges s estimated to be mere than 3,300 tons in weight), and lifts, to lower and raise barges and boats to and from the canals. And whilst the capitalists of the greater cities looked coldly upon the project when it was placed before thetn, the people of Lancashire, and especially the small companies, looked on it with-such favour that there are now 39,710 distinct holdings of shares—many being those ef stores, companies, &c. Up to the end of 1887 there had been allotted £7,383,020 worth of shares, and nearly a third of that sum had been paid up, a very considerable portion of which had been expended on the purchase of the Bridgewater and subsidiary navigations, on land, and on works. What this great project will do' for Lancashire and Cheshire, when completed, remains to be seen. The hopes of the promoters are that it will increase its trades and manufactures, and carry more cheaply products of present and of future industries. It is a bold venture, brought out by those who " love the land" and its commerce, and believe that water carriage is essential for the development of its resources, and to meet a growing international competition, They have faced the stern and long contest to obtain powers, and at last won; they are giving their capital to it; and they look beyond the picturesque present of the under- taking in construction to the future of completion, with satisfaction at what has been done, and hope for that ffiture.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. RUNCORN.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. RUNCORN.

Since operatiohs were commenced a few weeks ago, great progress has been made on this section at No Man's Land. A large coffer dam, in the form of a square, has been completed, and on Wednesday the work of laying the first foundation of concrete for the river wall was commenced. At this spot the bed of the river is of solid rock, and although the difficulty of driving piles was thus increased, it will forn a magni- ficent foundation for the wall. A second dam is nearly finished, and piles are being driven for a third, an evidence that the operation in the river via be pushed forward with all vigour. Work is indeed carried on between tides both night and day, the patent lucigen lights being used to dispel the darkness. The offices at Duke's Field are approaching completion, and will be commodious, comfortable, and convenient. Special accommodation has been made for Mr. Gregson, the agent. He is upon the scene at all hours of the night and day, and adjoining his office is a room that it is intended to fit up as a sitting room, with the addition of a comfortable camp bed. RUNCORN MISSION. A very enjoyable and interesting entertainment was held on Tuesday at the Mission Chapel. A service of song was given entitled "John Tregenoweth—His Mark" accompanied by magic lantern views depicting various scenesin the narrative. Mr. C. A. F. Gregson, the agent for this section, presided over the meeting, supported by Rev. R. Grims,on, M.A., chaplain to the whole of the Ship Canal Works. The descriptive read- ings were given by Mr. Gill, the cashier, and the singing portion was very effectively rendered by the Mission choir. Mr. Sharrock presided at the harmonium, and Mr. Jones acted as conducter. Solos by Mr. D. Smith, Miss Brown and Miss Clara Moore, and a duet by Miss Brown and Master E. Rhead were warmly applauded. The Chairman in his opening remarks complimented the men on the fact that he had seen less drunkenness on these works than on any other public works that he had previously superintended. The magic lantern was managed by Mr. H. Handley, who not only gave his services but also took a number of photographs of the staff and works which gave no small amount of pleasure to the persons present. The whole entertainment was a complete success givinggeneral satisfaction to a crowded and appreciative audience, composed largely of the men

employed on the works and their wives. It was brought to a close by a vote of thanks to all who had taken part, proposed by Mr. J. Watson, the resident missionary, and seconded by the Rev.. R. Grimston, M.A. MOORE AND ACTON GRANGE. A period of comparative inactivity, which is the natural result of the great progress made at the be- ginning of the year, has set in on the Moore section. The cutting for some distance is almost deserted, and most of the rails have been removed. The Acton Grange part, however, is kept busy, it being the centre point of operations for the two sections, and being a place where Important Dieces of work have to be done. STOCKTON HEATH AND WALTON.

At the ici;e7i.i;t of the works the German navvy removes spoil at a regular and quick rate. Two trains of twenty-one waggons are frequently filled in an hour. and large numbers of visitors watch,the rapid loading of the waggons with considerable surprise. The cutting at the Walton side of Chester-road is now within fifty yards of the row of houses near to Tons Payne's Bridge. A large pump is being taken up here, the soil absorbing the rain so quickly that it is not needed. LATCHFORD, THELWALL, /cc. There are now four navvies of the American type at work at the head of the cutting, one of which is commencing in the second lift, while the other three are engaged at the left bank in widening the excavation already made. The inroad of water caused by the backing up of the river, and the continuous heavy rains a few weeks ago, into the cutting, could not be over- come by the pumping apparatus which had been found hitherto sufficient. A pump of much greater capacity than any hitherto at work in this part of the excavation has been erected, and on its completion last week a few days sufficed to drain the canal cutting from Lymin to Thelwall of all surplus water. The water on the island known as Riston, or Wolff's Ley, is still a source of trouble. There are iarge fissures in the sandy sides of the cutting running from the surface downwards, said to be caused by long continued saturation, and it is thought they may communicate with the river. The German navvy at work here is not much affected by water, as, unlike the American, it does not require men to be in the trench to superintend the progress of the operations. The river, at the point where the canal cros-es at the Weir, is not yet stopped, though very nearly, and when this is accomplished the German navvy will work through Lymm meadows towards the river, crossing at the mouth of the Bollin. FATALITY AT IRLAM. Oa Monday morning Mr. F. Price, County Coroner, received information of the death of Daniel Spellar, rope runner, of Fidder's-lane, Irlam, from injuries received on the Ship Canal Works on Saturday. Deceased, who was 29 years of age, was employed on the Ship Canal Werks, an about half-past six o'clock on Saturday evening was riding on the foremost of 11 waggons loaded with coal, which were being pushed by an engine from the siding on the Cheshire Lines Railway, near Irlam Station, to the Ship Canal Works at Flixton. On going doWn the incline near Irlam Station deceased signalled to reverse the engine and pull back, as something was wrong. The driver, James Dumayne. did so, and the ganger, George king, ran to the front of the train, and found several of the waggons off the line, and deceased jammed between them. Another engine was obtained, and after about an hour deceased was liberated. He was taken to his home at Higher Irlam. a mile and a half away, where he died at about half-past ten the same evening. The -incline alluded to leads from the Che,shire Lines Railway to the Ship Canal Works.
DEBATE AT WIDNES LIBERAL CLUB.

The lecture room of the Widnes Liberal Club was on Thursday evening the scene of an interesting debate on the question of "The House of Lords; shall it be mended or ended," It is hoped to arrange a series of debates on political subjects during the win- ter, and the success of the first was very encourag- ing, Mr. J. Morrison undertook the duties of the " speaker " and the members ranged themselves on either side of the Howe. Mr. F. Hartland opened the proceedings with an able paper in favour of ending the House of Lords, which he _pointed out, at the outset, had been aboliga as uißess by resolution of the House of Commons on the 6th February 1649. One great evil of the House of Lords, he said, was that it was not an elective body and did not consider the wishes of the people. For 174 years no sovereign on the English throne had rejected a single measure that had passed the Houses of Parliament, but the Lords now did what the monarchs formerly did. Sir Charles Hake and Mr. John Bright were quoted, and the statement of Mr. Chamberlain was applauded—that during the last century the House of Lords had pro- teetad every abuse, and consolidated every privilege ; bad denied justice and delayed reform had been obstinate without courage, arbitrary without judgment, and arrogant without knowledge. The essayist showed by facts that the House of Lords failed to perform the Talmo function's it was supposed to possess, and inovea " Trial this 'meeting is ift favour of the total abolition of the House of Lords as being quite I unneccessary for the good Government of the coon- try."—Mr. J. Marsh moved an amendment that the upper chamber be Mended and not ended, that it be elected, by owners of property of the annual value or£2oo and upwards, that bishops be eligible, and that distinguished men be elected as life peers. Mr. Finn argued that the sooner the House of Lords was ended the better. Taking history throngh, there had not been a single beneficial measure introduced by the House of Commons that the House of Lords had not either strenuously opposed or rejected with allthe hatred, malignity,ancl -contempt it was possible to put into their hearts.—Mr. F. J. Poole contended that if the objection- able features were removed the House of Lords could be made extremely useful as a second chamber.- Even Cromwell after the resolution of abolition saw the neces- sity of a second chamber, and John Stuart Mill was an advocate in its favour. In America the second chamber had worked successfully forthe benefit of the country and there had been no tangible reason advanced why the House of Lords should lie ended completely. Destroy, the hereditary principle, and adopt the scheme of Lord Rosebery. by introducing the principle of election, and adding representatives from the Colonies, and the House of Lords would be brought within the influence of popular feeling, and be no longer the.upholder of one political party, and of one class —Mr. Shores delivered a highly sarcastic and amusing speech concluding amid loud laughter with the couplet— Though arts decay and wealth and commerce elle Save, oh save, our old nobility. Mr.ltoberts supported the motionin a capital speech and Mr. Fox spoke in favour of mendina, advocating the introduction of the elective principle, and the placing.of the Institution upon a foundation more in accordance with the democratic spirit of the age.— Mr. W. Ear land having replied, a division was taken, showing .14 in favour of " ending " and 10 in favour of mending. The motion was.therefore declared carried, and a'vote of thanks having been accorded to Mr. Hartland the proceedings terminated.

BRIGHT'S ILLNRSS.—On Thursday afternoon Mr. Bright was about the same as on the previous day, but the state of the lungs had improved. Dr. Hayle, wrote out this bulletin at half-past eight in the evening.—" Mr. Bright is about the same as on Wednesday night. His general strength is fairly sustained, and his lungs slightly improved." At three o'clock yesterday afternoon Dr. Hayle informed a correspondent that Mr. Bright had passed a fairly good night, and that his strength was fairly good. A Synatme TRAGEDT.—A strange story comes from Bolton. It is to the effect that a young man named Warburton, a shop porter, took a close of morphia on Thursday, was attended by a medical man, and pro- nounced lifeless. Four hours afterwards, when certain preparations had been made for his interment, signs of life were visible. Medical aid was again sought, but without avail, and the young man really died. It is said that he poisoned himself because of a disappointment in love. LIBERAL MEETING AT MANCHESTER.—A great Liberal demonstration was held in the Free Trade Hall, Man- chester, on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. H. J. Roby. Addresses were delivered by the Right Hon. H. Campbell-Bannerman, M.P., and Mr. J. E. Redmond, M.P. Mr. Campbell-Bannerman dealt with various points of the Edinburgh speech of Lord Salisbury. A resolution was passed unanimously protesting against the present administration of Ireland as incapable of remedying Irish grievances, hurtful to the good fame and interests of England, and tending to perpetuate the bad traditions of the past. Sir Wiliam Pearce was reported to be in a very critical condition last evening. Lord Salisbury has granted an abatement of 20 per cent, in the rents of his agricultural tenants.

Lord Wolseley was precluded on Thursday evening from presiding at 'a prize distribution in consequence of a very severe and sudden attack of illness. DESTRUCTIVE FIEES.—A galvation Army barracks and two warehouses were burnt down at Merthyr yesterday. The farm buildings of Mr. Thompson Binns, at Braith- waite, near Keighley, were burnt down yesterday morning, nine cows being roasted alive,

LATEST NEWS.

div.head: SHOCKING ACCIDENT : TWO MEN KILLED.
div.p: SHOCKING ACCIDENT : TWO MEN KILLED.

terrible accident occurred at the shuttle works of Messrs. Kirk and Co, Cobstall, Blackburn, yesterday morning, by which it is feared several men will lose, their lives. While the machinery was running in the upper rooms of the building, which is a very old one, the floor gave way without the slightest warning, and com- pletely buried the workmen underneath. A relief party, after working two hours, succeeded in bringing out the dead bodies of two Workmen, who were crushed almost 'beyond recognition. Both men are married and leave families.

div.head: MAIDSTONE ELECTION.
div.p: THE MAIDSTONE ELECTION.

The polling for the election of a Parliamentary repre- sentative of Maidstone commenced at eight o'clock on Friday morning, the candidates being Mr. John.' Barker (Gladstorlian Liberal), and Mr. Fiennes Stanley Wvlcehain Cornwallis (Conservative). There are 4,273 electors, and at the last election Major Ross (Conservative) secured a majority of 314. Vehicles of all kinds were employed, but the attendance was not large at first. The poll was declared last evening as follows : CORNWALLIS (C.) 2050 BARKER (0.L.) 1865
Majority lB5 At the last election, the Conservative majority was 314; It has now been reduced by 129 votes.
THE FATE OF STANLEY. LETTER FROM OSMAN DIGNA.

The " Standard" says: We have reason to believe that in the letter written by Osman Digna to the commander of the forces at Suakan it is stated that the troops des- patched by the Mandi against Emin Pasha had at length been successful. Emin Pasha held out bravely to the last, but his men mutinied, and delivered him up. together with the "White Traveller," to the Mandist leader. The "White Man" is believed to be Mr. Stanley. Osman Digna sends with his letter proofs which tend to support the truth of his assertions. Canto, FRIDAY.—The letter received by General Grenfell from Osman Digna contains details of the sur- render to the Mandists of the Equatorial Province and the capture of Emin Pasha and a "white traveller" at Lado. Enclosed was a copy of a letter addressed to the Khalifa by the dervish leader at Lado, giving the date of the surrender as October 10. Osman Digna's communi- cation also contained a letter taken from the -"white traveller," which is apparently a copy of the Khedive's letter to Emin Pasha, dated February 2, 1817, given by his Highness to Mr. Stanley when the latter passed through Cairo. THE CABINET AND THE NEWS.

_ The reported capture of Emin Pasha and Stanley by Osman Digna is believed to be true, though no official announcement has yet been made, and much excitement is caused thereby. It is understood that Osman is willing to release Emin and Stanley provided he has substantial concession amounting to the Egyptian aban- donment of Suakim.. Unless Arab demands are complied With, Emin and Stanley would receive little mercy. Osman's letter was considered by the Cabinet Council yesterday afternoon.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S ' PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S ' PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met at one o'clock. A new writ was issued for Stockton. Mr. STEWART WORTLEY, replying to Mr. C. KENNY, said it was intended next Session to introduce a Bill to render the Infant Life Protection Act more efficient in the suppression of baby farming. Mr. W. Sarum, replying to Mr. JOHN MORLEY, said instructions ave been forwarded to ;he military commanders at Suakim in conformity with assurances given by the Marquis of Salisbury. THE FATE OF STANLEY.—Sir W. LAWSON asked whether General Grenfell had received a letter from Osman Digna, and whether there was any truth in the report that Emin Bey and Stanley were. in the hands of the Mandi. Mr. W. &mu said they knew of the letter by telegraph. It contained statements as to the surrender of Emin Bey, and of a "White Traveller," but the Government had no means of knowing whether the allegations were well founded. Lord It. CHURCHILL asked whether Government would enter into negotiations for the release of Emin Bey and the "White Traveller "before commencing hostilities. Mr. W. Smrrit asked that the question might be put on Mon- day. Mr. E. STANHOPW,' in reply-to Mr. Du.tow, said there was an arrangement between her Majesty's Government and the Khedive, by which the cost of fresh reinforcements would be borne by the Egyptian Govern- ment. EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY hat—Mr. SIMI= intimated that in consequence of the serious opposition to the further progress of the Employers' Liability Bill the Government were under the necessity of relinquishing all hope of proceeding with the Bill this Session. Steps would be taken to continue the present Act.

SIIPPLY.—AnNY EsrmArns.—A vote for the medical establishment was proposed, after conversation between Mr. H. FOWLES, Mr.-E. SrAnnosn,Lord it. Cauxictuu.. and Mr. CHILDERS. It was agreed not to enter into dis- cussion of recommendations of the Committee on Army Estimates. Dr. FARQUHARSON, proceeding with the Con- sideration of the vote, colsidered that a Medical Officer of the Army should not be disqualified by one failure in the examination for promotion to Rank of Brigade Surgeon. Mr. STANHOPE said in the absence of new facts he could not depart from the attitude he had already taken on the subject. After further conversa- tion, the vote was agreed to.—The votes for militia, yeo- manry cavalry, and , army reserve were agreed to.— During discussion on miscellaneous charges for war office, Colonel Nonsn said he thought many things were purchased by the director of contracts above market value. He believed it would lead to C great saving of public money if more articles were purchased by open competition. -- After further discussion the vote 3 was agreed to, as were the remaining army votes. ritFT SITTINGI '

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

BRITISH AND FOREIGN Buns SOCIETY.—On Monday the annual meeting in aid of this society was held in the boys' schoolroom, at Kingsley, where an address on," The Bible" was delivered by the Rot. Jellinger E. Symons, of Southport. The Vicar (Rev. A. P. Reynolds) presided. The rev. gentleman's remarks were illustrated by means of diagrams. At the close of the lecture, a collection was made in aid of the society's funds. KINGSLEY LIBERAL COMMItTEE.—Last evening week a public meeting, convened by the members of this Committee was held at the Primitive Methodist School- room, when a lecture on " Irish Evictions "was delivered by the Rev. B. Kniveton, of Rune,crn. Mr. P. Hall, Kingsley, occupied the chair. The speaker touched upon some of the leading features in the Irish land question, ' and its bearing upon crime, the Plan of Campaign, &c. Mr. Shore, of Runcorn, supported the lecturer's remarks. At the close a vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman and speaker by-Mr. S. Woodward, seconded by Mr. E. Alderman.

FRODSHAM Musient SOCIETY—On Tuesday evening the first concert of the eighth season of the Frodsham Musical Society was held in the Town Hall, the principals being Miss K. S. Rigby, Mrs. Webster, Mr. James Kent, and Mr. J. Austin. The first part of the programme comprised S. T. Coleridge's cantata "The Ancient Mariner," and was sung by. the members of the society with string band accompaniments, together with harmonitim and pianoforte, the performers numbering altogether about fifty. The National Anthem brought a successful concert to a close. Mr. J. R, CurnoW was the conductor, whilst Mr. C. H. Hibbert and Mr. Howick presided at the piano and harmonium respec- tively. • FOREIGN MISSIONARY MERTING.—A public meeting was held in the Union Church, Frodsham Bridge, in behalf of the foreign missions, on Monday evening. Mr. Samuel Rigby, of Chester, presided. Mr. T. A. Rigby explained that the meeting was the first of the kind held on the new premises, and during the past two years the various collections taken from time to time had been devoted to the paying off of the debt on the premises. He, how- ever, now had the pleasure of declaring the church free from such incumbrance, and after the accomplishment of this object, the friends considered that the first collec- tions taken afterwards should be given to the mission cause. The Rev. Harry Scott, late of New Guinea, gave an acceunt of the natives of that part of the world, and was followed by the Rev. John Marriott, a missionary from Samoa. At the close a vote of thanks was given to the deputation on ' the motion of Mr. Samuel Ormrod, seconded by MI.. F. Beck.

A Mullingar correspondent reports some "miracles," which are alleged to have been wrought by Canon Larkin, ftom Surrey. The rev, gentleman was fol- lowed to Mullingar by a number of persons from Cavan, where he is said to have cured the deaf, lame and blind. THEFT OF TOBACCO AT EARLESTOWN.—At an Occasional Court held at Warrington, on Monday, a boy Ramed Eclward Bailey, of no settled abode, was brought up pn a charge of having stolen four ounces of tobacco from the shop of George Pennington, Market-street, Earlestown. On the sth inst., according to the evidence, prisoner and some other boys went into Pennington 's shop, and one of them made a trifling purchase. When they had gone Mrs. Pennington missed four ounces of tobacco, and it was afterwards ascertained that prisoner had taken them. Prisoner, who has been in a reformatory, and who has a bad character, , was committed to the Liverpool Assizes for trial.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE DARESBURY LADIES AND 0 ENTLEMEN,—I have been requested to come forward as a candidate for your division in the new -County Council, and I feel that on public grounds it is my duty to comply with such request. I have been connected with your division for nearly half a century, and I am fully conversant with the rights and interests of the ratepayers in relation to County matters. I consider that all rates levied for County purposes should be under the control of a body responsible to the ratepayers, and should be administered economically in the interests of such ratepayers. The Act constituting the Council, takes out of the hands of the Justices of the Peace all matters relating to County gov- ernment, with the exception of criminal administration, appeals, &c., and a joint control of the police by a committee formed of certain Justices and certain members of the County Council ; all other County business will be in the hands of the new Council. The public positions which I hold, and my general know- ledge of public business, justify use in sayinq that I should be able to render valuable services to the ratepayers of the county, and it is upon this ground, and not from any personal ambi- tion. that I am desirous for a seat upon the Council. There are certain matters affecting the interest and con- venience of occupiers of land and owners of stock which require amendment, so as to avoid the inconvenience at present existing as to the transfer of stock from one part of the county to another, and the regulations under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, require, I think,very careful revision. If I am returned for your division I shall at all times publicly ventilate all matters which may prejudicially affect the constituency of the Daresbury Division. I am, Ladies and Gentleme Yours faithfully, H. LI NAKER. Frodsham, 6th December, 1888.

CHESHIRE COUNTY, COUNCIL. T O THE ELECTORS OF TIIE NORTH DIVISION • OF RUNCORN. LADIES and GENTLEMEN.—Some three weeks ago by a short paragraph in the local papers I pledged myself to come forward as a candidate for this Division, in the new County Council, and I now beg to confirm that announcement. The County Councils throughout the country have been called into existence in compliance with a demand which has from time to time been urged upon successive Governments by all parties, the feeling generally being that the ratepayers of the counties should have a voice in the election of some directly representative bodies which should leave the control not only of all county property but also of the making, assessing, and levying of all county, bridge, aad other rates, 'which up to the present time have been under the control of I Quarter Sessions. This the new Local Government Act— although imperfect in many ways—fully admits and pro- vides for. In the future the County Councils will have under their control the making and levying of all county, polieeand bridge rates, and the full control over all county property, from shire halls, and assize courts, county asylums, reformatories and industrial schools, down to police courts. The Court of Quarter Sessions will retain little more than the administration of their criminal jurisdiction, appeals, &c. The police will be placed under the control of a joint com- mittee of a certain number of justices, and a certain number of members of the County Council. On this point as well as upon many others it willbe neces- sary to see that the interests of the public are protected, and I think that by the direct representation which ratepayers generally will now obtain, many evils and petty annoyances will be removed. It is impossible in an address of this kind to touch upon all the powers conferred by the new Act upon the Council, and have only referred to a few of the most important. My justification in asking you to support my candidature in this election is that from the public position in which I have been placed for many years in the connection with your local body of Commissioners and the Runcorn Union, I have acquired a ,ltnowledge of local and county matters which will assist me materially in protecting the interests of your Division, and of the district generally. I promise one thing, that nothing 4 shall be done by the Council but what is thoroughly investi- gated and made known to the public. Liam no personal interest in seeking your support; I ask it in the interests of your Division. lam, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, W. H. LINAKER. 58, High-st.„ Runcorn, 13th December, 1888.

DENSE FOG.-EXTRAORDINARY FATALITIES. A dense fog hung over London oil Tuesday morning from daytiglit, and, especially on the south side of the Thames, was so thick that traffic became congested. The river service was almost entirely suspended, and on the railways there was scarcely less interruption of traffic. Locometion in the streets was difficult- A thick fog, prevailea in London and suburbs on Tues- day, the atmosphere being raw and cold. A fog gathered on Sunday in the lower parts of the Metropolitan dis- trict, and thickened as the night advanced, there being considerable hoar frost on Monday. Traffic in the streets was carried on with difficulty, while trades on the rail- ways were much delayed. On the river it was found neeessary to stop nearly all traffic, as there the fog was T • fog was very dense at Glasgow on Tuesday, and fo men walked into the river Clyde and were drowned. Their sties for help were heard, but they could not be seen in the darkness. Sile other men fell into the river at various places on the bank, but were all rescued and taken to the Glasgow police office, where restoratives were applied successfully. The fog stopped all naviga- tion on the Clyde on Monday night., but about 30 steamers got out on Tuesday. Sour vessels are ashore near Dumbarton. aa, CURRENT rouTrcs. • The Press Association learns en nuthority that Parlia- meat will be prorogued on Monday, the 24th inst. Mr. and Mrs..6ladstone vistted be Royalty Theatre, Chester, on Saturday night, to see " The Taming of the Shrew." Crowds eV-tiered both outside and in th e theatre, and the right hon. gentleman had a splendid reception. The hon. secretary of the Liverpool Parnell expenses fund has received £4O, on'acconnt, from Mr. Drongan, secretary of the Home Rule Clnb, Batton, being the first amount received by the Liverpool committee from an Irish association in Great Britain. Mr. Gaiusford Bruce, who took his seat the other day, is the sixty-first new member returned to the present Parliament. ' The present House contains only 30 mem- bers who held seats prior to the election of 1868. Of these 14 are Liberals, 12 Conservatives, and four Dissen- tient.Liberals. IVales contribrites three members to this ever-diminishing hand—Mr. aflwyn, Sir Hussey Vivian, and Mr. Talbot, "Father of the House," who has sat for Glatnorganshire during the uninterrupted period of 58 years. LORD R. CHURCHILL AND THE SUAKIN! DIVISION. Lord Randolph Churchill replies to a letter addressed to him on the subject of his nation for the adjournment of the House of Commons, on Tuesday, in order that he might draw attention to theposition of affairs at Suakim. His object Is to vindicate himself from the suspicion of having desired to snatch a surprise division and to de- feat the Government. He regrets to say that with the exception of himself end some half-dozen others, there is not a single Conservative member of the Conservative party who can reconcile his action in the recent debates on Suakim with the action taken in Parliament and on the platform by the whole Tory party. LORD SALISBURY AND THE "BLACK MAN." The feeling about Lord Salisbury's refer ence to Mr. Naoroji is growing in intensity. There was at first, a disposition among members of Parliament to allow the matter to be dealt with by extra-Parliamentary opinion, but there is now an idea that the question should he brought before Parliament. So far as this country is concerned, the matter might safely be left to public opinion out of doors. Lord Salisbury, however, to the people of India appears as the representative of the Im- perial Government, and it is desirable that they should know how deeply his language is resented.
